title: Directory of Communication Related Mental Measures
rights: The rights to the text are held by Jason S. Wrench (confirmed 2026-11-17). The directory describes published measures; it does not reproduce their items.

introduction.text: A Brief History of Mental Measures

The history of the social sciences is very much dependent on the scientific community’s understanding of measurement. Darwin’s (2003/1859) publication of The Origin of Species drew attention to the notion of genetic variation, or the notion that nature selects certain traits and attributes to be passed from one generation to the next while others are not. Darwin’s work on genetic variation spurred the drive to scientifically measure individual differences. Darwin’s half cousin Francis Galton (1869) was the first scientist to tackle this task, which culminated in the publication of his book Hereditary Genius. In Hereditary Genius, Galton applied Darwin’s ideas to humans by demonstrating “that a man’s natural abilities are derived by inheritance, under exactly the same limitations as are the form and physical features of the whole organic world” (p.1). Galton realized that he needed to develop a way to assess an individual’s genius, so he decided to examine an individual’s fame in his career and see how his children fared in their careers. This crude attempt at measuring a non-physical attribute is the first time an individual attempted to measure something social scientifically. Ultimately, Galton demonstrated that individuals who were famous in their careers had children who were also famous in their careers. Hereditary Genius created the field of quantitative differential psychology, or the study of how individuals or groups differ.

While Galton was primarily interested in measuring genetic differences among people, American psychologist James McKeen Cattell (1890) traveled to England to learn how Galton used statistics to understand humans. In 1890, Cattell was the first social scientist to develop measurements for non-physical attributes. Cattell’s justification for his project was very simple, “Psychology cannot attain the certainty and exactness of the physical sciences, unless it rests on a foundation of experiment and measurement” (p. 373). Cattell realized that the social sciences had come to a crossroad. One road to be taken would eventually lead to the development of the humanities as we know it today, but the second road would eventually lead to the scientific exploration of human behavior. To take this step in a measurement oriented direction, Cattell recommended the following:

A step in this direction could be made by applying a series of mental tests and measurements to a large number of individuals. The results would be of considerable scientific value in discovering the constancy of mental processes, their interdependence, and their variation under different circumstances. Individuals, besides, would find their tests interesting, and, perhaps, useful in regard to training, mode of life or indication of disease. (p. 373)

Cattell initiated his process of developing mental tests and measures by first looking at ten specific variables: dynamometer pressure, rate of movement, sensation-areas, pressure causing pain, least noticeable difference in weight, reaction-time for sound, time for naming colors, bi-section of a 50 centimeter line, judgment of 10 seconds time, and number of letters remembered on once hearing. While these variables may seem slightly rudimentary to today’s laundry list of social-scientific variables, these ten variables would eventually create a firestorm of research among psychologists, sociologists, and eventually communication researchers.

During his tenure at the University of Pennsylvania, Cattell began to administer newly developed measures to students, which he ultimately labeled “mental tests” or “mental measures.” The term “mental measures” is used today to refer to any “tool used for the measurement of mental functions like attitudes, beliefs, cognitive knowledge, perceived knowledge, personality/behavioral traits, and psychological functioning” (Wrench, Thomas-Maddox, Richmond, & McCroskey, 2008, p. 171). Basically, any achievement test, personality test, aptitude test, intelligence test, or career choice test qualifies as a mental measure (Salkind, 2006). By the time the 20th century rolls around, mental measurement began picking up steam both in the United States and around the world.

In 1905, Alfred Binet, a French psychologist, was commissioned to create the first test to determine if children were functioning at lower than normal levels. Binet, along with his doctoral student Theodore Simon, created the Binet-Simon Scale, which measured a child’s adeptness at completing various age appropriate tasks (Binet, 1905). The Binet-Simon Scale became the first known intelligence test of its kind. Binet’s research was then furthered by Stanford University professor Lewis Terman (1916) who furthered intelligence testing to examine intelligence as a function that could be measured for everyone. During World War I, the American Psychological Association along with Lewis Terman volunteered to create a test of verbal (for illiterate recruits) and nonverbal (for literate recruits) tests of intelligence for the U.S. army. The tests became known as Army Alpha (verbal) and Army Beta (nonverbal). In the next two decades, intelligence testing became academic achievement testing, which culminated in the 1937 creation of the Stanford Achievement Test (SAT) that was required for entry into Ivy League schools. By 1947 so many people were taking educational tests, the Educational Testing Service (ETS) was ultimately created to oversee the production, psychometrics, and distribution of educational tests, which still oversees numerous tests today.

While educational tests and basic psychological functioning tests were very dominant during the 1890s and first decade of the 1900s, personality testing really did not occur until the end of World War I. While the Army Alpha (verbal) and Army Beta (nonverbal) intelligence tests were useful, the army additionally wanted a mental measure that could determine the psychological state of new recruits beyond their intelligence. To aid in the creation of such a measure, Robert Woodworth (1920) was commissioned by the American Psychological Association on behalf of the U.S. military to create a measure of emotional stability that could be used to test new recruits. Woodworth ultimately created the Woodworth Personal Data Sheet, which contained a series of 116 “yes” “no” questions. Unfortunately, the test was developed too late in WWI to be used in the screening of new recruits, but the test did become the forerunner of future personality tests (Segal & Coolidge, 2003). Eventually, this test would become the first mental measure to measure a personality variable on large numbers of participants under its new name, the Wadsworth Psychoneurotic Questionnaire.
In 1918, William Isaac Thomas and Florian Znaniecki defined social psychology as “the study of attitudes.” Along with the development of attitudinal research, Jowett and O’Donnell (1992) note:

Other social sciences such as sociology and psychology were also stimulated by the need to pursue questions about human survival in an age in which social strain grew heavy with concerns about warfare, genocide, economic depression, and human relationships. These questions were about influence, leadership, decision making, and changes in people, institutions, and nations. Such questions were also related to the phenomena of propaganda, public opinion, attitude change, and communication. (p. 123)

The study of attitudes ultimately opened up a series of new mental measure formats that became popular over the rest of the 20th century. While psychologists and sociologists have relied on a wide range of differing mental measure formats, communication scholars have relied primarily on two formats: the Likert Scale and the Semantic-Differential Scale.

Rensis Likert (1932) published an article based on his dissertation in which he developed a new attitude-scaling technique from a survey of student attitudes. The basic premise of the Likert scale was quite simplistic, but ultimately revolutionized social scientific research. Likert started off with the idea of presenting respondents a declarative statement of some kind (e.g., “The president is doing a good job”); then offer the respondents a range of possible choices (strongly disagree, disagree, neither agree or disagree, agree, or strongly agree); and finally requiring that the respondent select one and only one choice. The range of choices have weighted distances, so the answer on a single Likert item is considered ordinal because researchers cannot assume that respondents perceive the difference between the different levels evenly. However, when the multiple Likert items are summed together, the summed total may be treated as interval data that actually measures a latent construct.

The next truly major breakthrough in the area of attitudinal measurement came from Osgood (1952) and Osgood, Tannnenbaum, and Suci (1957). Stanger and Osgood (1946) were examining people’s social stereotypes. To examine these social stereotypes associated with particular concepts like “pacifist, Russian, dictator, and neutrality,” Stanger and Osgood presented a series of oppositely worded adjectives to their respondents with a 7-step scale in between the two adjectives. Previous research by Karwoski, Odbert, and Osgood (1942) had presented respondents with a set of oppositely worded adjectives and asked the respondents to just pick one of the adjectives. Stanger and Osgood, however, realized that it may be useful if a continuum existed between the two adjectives to show gradients of meaning. Ultimately, Stanger and Osgood’s scale became known as a semantic differential scale.

A semantic differential scale asks respondents to rate their opinion on a linear scale between two endpoints that have opposite meanings (e.g., Good/Bad, Dirty/Clean, Slow/Fast, Weak/Strong, Light/Heavy, Moral/Immoral, etc.). Between these two oppositely worded adjectives, there exists a series of steps. The most common number of steps in a semantic-differential scale is seven, so instructions for a semantic differential test read like this “Circle the number between the adjectives which best represents your beliefs. Numbers ‘1’ and ‘7’ indicate a very strong feeling. Numbers ‘2’ and ‘6’ indicate a strong feeling. Numbers ‘3’ and ‘5’ indicate a fairly weak feeling. Number ‘4’ indicates you are undecided or do not understand the adjectives themselves.” Whether or not we actually have the physical numbers present in a semantic differential really isn’t important as long as we, as the researchers, know that we have direct quantifiable distances between each step. Since these steps are weighted distances, the answer on a single Semantic-Differential item is considered ordinal because researchers cannot assume that respondents perceive the difference between the steps evenly. However, if multiple Semantic Differential items are summed together, the summed total may be treated as interval data that actually measures a latent construct.

Today there are literally hundreds of thousands of mental tests and measures that exist. There are also two online databases that can be useful when searching for mental measures: Mental Measures Yearbook and Educational Testing Service. By 1938, there were so many new mental-measures being developed that Oscar K. Buros decided to publish the first volume of the Mental Measures Yearbook. The Mental Measures Yearbook attempts to locate and provide descriptions of the measure, one or two reviews of the measure, and references for how to find the measure. The Buros Center for Testing (http://www.unl.edu/buros/) is still an active research center for mental measures, and the 17th volume of the Mental Measures Yearbook came out in 2007 (Gesinger, Spies, Carlson, & Plake).

The Educational Testing Service (http://www.ets.org/) also has started compiling mental measures. If you are on the ETS’s website, click on the link that says “Find a Test.” You will be taken to the Test Directory homepage. You will need to scroll down until you find the link to “Test Link,” which is a database of over 25,000 mental measures. In fact, in a simple name search there are over 160 mental measures with the word “communication” in the title alone. On the ETS website, you can also order many tests for $25 a pop, but often the location of the physical test or contact information for the test’s creator is also available.

Beyond just websites there is the Mental Measures Yearbook and the Directory of Unpublished Experimental Mental Measures published by the American Psychological Association (Goldman & Mitchell, 2003). While both of these publications contain mental measures related to communication, as of yet there is not a directory of mental measures specifically for communication related measures. The current project hopes to fill this void. A directory of mental measures is not a list or critiques of the scales themselves. If you are looking for critiques of communication scales, we would recommend Rubin, Palmgreen, and Sypher (2004), which was originally published in 1991. Instead, this Directory of Communication Related Mental Measures is a list of current measures in existent within the field. To create this directory, the following journals have been consulted:
Journal of Business and Technical Communication
Journal of Language and Social Psychology
Journal of Marriage and the Family
The Speech Teacher (see also Communication Education)

If in the process of our search for communication related mental measures we found a measure outside one of these journals, we examined the original article and have included the mental measure’s citation within this directory. In a couple of cases, highly utilized scales within the field of communication were not originally published within a journal (ex., Personal Report of Communication Apprehension-24) but has been utilized in numerous research studies, so we felt it was necessary to include the original citation and any relevant citations within journals as well.
The directory is broken down in a variety of categories designed to be similar to the interest group structure in existent with the National Communication Association:

The placement of a specific mental measure was not always as clear as it should be, so we apologize up front for our classification of different measures. For example, Wrench and Richmond’s (2004) Humor Assessment Inventory was originally published in a format for instructional purposes, so the mental measure could be classified as an instructional context measure. However, the measure has been utilized primarily to examine the use of humor during communicative interactions (Wrench & McCroskey, 2001), so the measure was listed as an interaction trait measure. If you are looking for a specific measure, we recommend looking in the index. While we scoured the physical copies of literally thousands of volumes of academic journals looking for mental measures, we are sure that some mental measures have been missed. Accept our apologies for this oversight and please let us know so we can include missed measures in future editions of this directory (wrenchj@newpaltz.edu).

For a mental measure to be included within this directory, the measure had to be available in full-text within a peer-reviewed academic journal. We did not include professionally published mental measures because these generally require payment to the publisher or author for use in academic research, which is a practice the authors of this book find reprehensible. To aid you in your search for useful mental measures, we have provided the following information for each mental measure in the directory if presented in the original article: test name, purpose, number of items, format, original sample, reliability, validity, brief critique, source, related research, and categories. We have chosen this format for a few reasons. First, this format resembles the format used by the American Psychological Association in the publication of its Directory of Unpublished Experimental Mental Measures. By following the same format as the APA, we hope to encourage people who are familiar with their publication to use this publication as well. Second, the information provided gives you the basic information about the psychometric properties of the mental measure. Lastly, the information provided is the basic information a researcher needs to find the full-text of the mental measure and pertinent related research. Once you have found a mental measure you think will be beneficial to your research, simply pull the original article cited as the source and you will find the full-text version of the scale. We have opted not to include full-text measures within this directory because of the expense that doing so would cause. Now that we have explained the basic reasoning behind the format of this directory, we can look at the different sections of an individual mental measure’s citation.

The name of the mental measure that is listed in the directory is the one given to the mental measure by the author of the original source. Therefore, it is possible that numerous sources will have very similar names if not the same name. If a mental measure was not named by the original author, the authors of this directory have provided a name.

Each mental measure is provided a concise statement explaining what the measure purports to measure. These statements are either taken directly from the author’s own words or are determined by the authors of this directory based on the scale items themselves. When necessary, further information is provided about the measure if it has been used in a variety of different contexts.
Each citation contains the number of items used by the mental measure. If a measure contains multiple factors, the citation includes the number of items used to measure each factor.

Each citation explains what kind of format is used by the mental measure (Likert Scale, Semantic-Differential, Thurstone, Scalogram, etc…). If a mental measure includes more than one format, both formats are discussed. If the measure contains a format that lies outside of traditional measurement, more detail is provided as necessary.
The original sample for each scale is discussed. Aspects of the sample that are included (if in the articles) are age, biological sex, ethnicity, and origin of the sample.

When reported by the measure’s author, the mental measure’s alpha reliability, split-half reliability, or test-retest reliability is given. If a mental measure’s reliability is not discussed, the authors of the directory note that “no reliability coefficients were provided in the article.”

When reported by the measure’s author, the mental measure’s validity will be discussed. Specifically, we address issues of a measure’s construct or factorial/context validity and a measure’s criterion validity (predictive, concurrent, & retrospective). If validity is not expressly discussed in an article, we will provide noted relationships between the newly created mental measure and other mental measures within the study. If there are no clear relationships as a possible indication of concurrent validity, the authors will note that “validity was not specifically discussed in this article.”

The critiques provided are as objective as humanly possible. As the authors of the Directory of Communication Related Mental Measures we did not think it was our place to discuss the actual utility of various measures beyond psychometric related issues. There are many mental measures that are included in this volume that we think are seriously flawed, however we kept our personal opinions out of our critiques. Some of the measures were also created for highly specific purposes, so we try to offer suggestions for how various measures could be utilized in other research projects.

The source is the original citation for the full-text version of the mental measure. In the case where a mental measure was originally found in a published book or unpublished paper and then utilized in research within an academic journal, both the book or conference paper and the journal citations are listed. However, books and unpublished papers are listed as related research.

Most mental measures do not exist in a vacuum, so we will provide related research when possible. This research could either relate to previous studies that informed the development of the mental measure, or studies that have utilized the mental measure. However, we limited reporting of related research to specific source materials necessary for research purposes, so do not expect an exhaustive list of research utilizing a specific measure.

Since numerous communication related mental measures do not fall into one specific category, we have listed all applicable categories. For example, the Personal Report of Interethnic Communication Apprehension (PRECA) is listed as both communication apprehension and intercultural communication since the scale can be used by scholars examining both areas. However, the PRECA is cited in the Communication Apprehension & Avoidance chapter, but also lists intercultural communication as a secondary category.

We hope this Directory of Communication Related Mental Measures will be a useful tool for your research endeavors. Within this first volume, we have profiled over 500 mental measures that have been published within communication journals. Many hours have gone into searching for mental measures, describing the mental measures, and categorizing the mental measures. However, we may have made mistakes along the way. If you find a mistake in this directory, please contact the lead author so we can correct these mistakes in future editions.

Lastly, the authors of this project did not undertake the creation of the Directory of Communication Related Mental Measures for our personal monetary gain. All of the funds generated by this book will help undergraduate students traveling to the National Communication Association Convention. We believe that our undergraduates will one day be our future colleagues, so exposing them to the NCA convention is a great way to demonstrate what it really means to be an academic professional. For this reason, please do not just copy this book and had it out to peers and students. When you make copies of this book and hand them out to people, you are preventing NCA from helping the next generation of communication scholars.

entries.name: Adult Communication Behaviors
entries.purpose: To assess the amount and types of communication adults typically engage in.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 20 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Participants were asked to estimate the number of times they had engaged in each item in the previous two years.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 218 participants recruited in two different communities for a telephone interview.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: The sample size is large enough for generalizability purposes. The measure does have three notable problems. First, the author did not report the anchors utilized in the measuring of the scale items. Second, reliability coefficients were not presented nor discussed in the article. Third, the validity of the measure is unknown. Future research should confirm factor analysis before using the scale.
entries.source: Tuttle, G. E. (1984). A field based model for determining adult communication behaviors. Communication Education, 33, 272-283.
entries.sourceApa7: Tuttle, G. E. (1984). A field based model for determining adult communication behaviors. Communication Education, 33(3), 272–283. https://doi.org/10.1080/03634528409384752
entries.referenceCheck: DOI and issue number from Crossref; title and year agree.

entries.name: Audience Responses To Performance Scale
entries.purpose: To measure audience responses to the performance of literary texts.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 17 Likert items.
entries.format: The exact anchors used in the study were not provided.
entries.originalSample: 304 audience members of a performance
entries.reliability: Cronbach alphas were .70 for Plans to Read the Book, .72 for Performance Program, .73 for Audience Discussion, and .38 for Buy the Book
entries.validity: Validity was not discussed in this study. However, a principal components analysis yielded a five factor model accounting for 63.2% of the variance. The fifth factor was deemed unreliable.
entries.critique: The sample size is large enough for generalizability purposes. Reliability coefficients for three factors were within the minimally acceptable and respectable ranges. However, one factor was unacceptable. The author noted that the scale should be revised for future research. Any research using this measure in future should attempt to improve the low reliability.
entries.source: Valentine, K. B., Hecht, M. L., Corey, F., & Jacobsen, J. L. (1995). Two measures of audience response to performance. Communication Reports, 8, 170-177.
entries.sourceApa7: Valentine, K. B., Hecht, M. L., Corey, F., & Jacobsen, J. L. (1995). Two measures of audience response to performance. Communication Reports, 8(2), 170–177. https://doi.org/10.1080/08934219509367623
entries.referenceCheck: DOI and issue number from Crossref; title and year agree.

entries.name: Interviewee Verbal Characteristics
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate an interviewer’s perception of an interviewee’s verbal characteristics.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 15 semantic differential items measuring four factors: speaker intelligence and competence (6 items), speaker’s agreeableness (4 items), speaker’s self-assurance (2 items), and Anglo-like (1 item).
entries.format: There are seven steps between the adjective pairs.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 12 employment interviewers who listened to four tape recorded interviews.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis accounted for 66.4% of the variance in the four factor model.
entries.critique: The sample size is not large enough for generalizability purposes. Second, reliability coefficients were not presented nor discussed in the article. Future research should confirm the reliability of the measure. Furthermore, there is not a clear indication that the sample size was adequate for performing a confirmatory factor analysis.
entries.source: Hopper, R., & Williams, F. (1973). Speech characteristics and employability. Speech Monographs, 40, 296-302.
entries.sourceApa7: Hopper, R., & Williams, F. (1973). Speech characteristics and employability. Speech Monographs, 40(4), 296–302. https://doi.org/10.1080/03637757309375807
entries.referenceCheck: DOI and issue number from Crossref; title and year agree.

entries.name: Narrative Coherence And Fidelity Measure
entries.purpose: To measure the coherence and fidelity of storytelling.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 22 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Nine point ranging from 1 (agree) to 9 (disagree)
entries.originalSample: 41 public speaking students. No other information about the sample was provided.
entries.reliability: Cronbach alphas were .77 for coherence and .82 for fidelity
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: First, the sample size is a little small, which could lead to problems accurately factor analyzing the scale items due to sampling adequacy problems. The scale reliability for narrative coherence was respectable and the scale reliability for fidelity was good. However, the validity of the measure is unknown. Future research should employ factor analysis to confirm the validity of the measure.
entries.source: Baesler, J. E. (1995). Construction and test of an empirical measure for narrative coherence and fidelity. Communication Reports, 8, 97-105.
entries.sourceApa7: Baesler, J. E. (1995). Construction and test of an empirical measure for narrative coherence and fidelity. Communication Reports, 8(2), 97–105. https://doi.org/10.1080/08934219509367615
entries.referenceCheck: DOI and issue number from Crossref; title and year agree.

entries.name: Perceptions Of Verbal Speech
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess an individual’s perception of a child’s verbal behavior.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 15 semantic differential items measuring two subscales: confidence/eagerness communicating (5 items) and ethnicity/non-standard English (5 items). An additional 5 items were filler.
entries.format: There are seven steps between the adjective pairs.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 44 undergraduate education majors who were presented with four audio clips represented standard and ethnically specific speech patterns of children.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: First, the sample size is a little small, which could lead to problems accurately factor analyzing the scale items due to sampling adequacy problems. The reliability and validity of the instrument are unknown. Future research should employ factor analysis to confirm reliability coefficients and the validity of the instrument.
entries.source: Williams, F., Whitehead, J. L., Miller, L. M. (1971). Ethnic stereotyping and judgments of children’s speech. Speech Monographs, 38, 166-170.
entries.sourceApa7: Williams, F., Whitehead, J. L., & Miller, L. M. (1971). Ethnic stereotyping and judgments of children’s speech. Speech Monographs, 38(3), 166–170. https://doi.org/10.1080/03637757109375706
entries.referenceCheck: DOI and issue number from Crossref; title and year agree.

entries.name: Perceived Vocal Behavior
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess individual’s perceptions of a source’s vocal behavior.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 22 semantic differential items measuring three subscales: competence (8 items), social attractiveness (8 items), and benevolence (6 items).
entries.format: There are five steps between the adjective pairs.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 42 individuals rating a series of 36 altered speech patterns.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation accounted for 84% of the variance in the two factor model.
entries.critique: First, the sample size is a little small, which could lead to problems accurately factor analyzing the scale items due to sampling adequacy problems. Second, reliability coefficients for the scale are unknown. Lastly, future research should employ factor analysis to examine reliabilities for the three factors.
entries.source: Hart, R. J., & Brown, B. L. (1974). Interpersonal information conveyed by content ad vocal aspects of speech. Speech Monographs, 41, 371-380.
entries.sourceApa7: Hart, R. J., & Brown, B. L. (1974). Interpersonal information conveyed by content ad vocal aspects of speech. Speech Monographs, 41(4), 371–380. https://doi.org/10.1080/03637757409375862
entries.referenceCheck: DOI and issue number from Crossref; volume, first page and year agree (the title is worded a little differently).

entries.name: Speech Dialectic Attitude Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine individual differences in perception as a result of source variations in dialect.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 21 semantic differential items measuring three subscales: socio-intellectual status (7 items), aesthetic quality (8 items), and dynamism (6 items).
entries.format: There are seven steps between the adjective pairs.
entries.originalSample: The first sample consisted of 370 people used across five different experimental conditions examining a variety of socio-linguistic attributes.
entries.reliability: Reliabilities ranged from .94 to .98 across the samples.
entries.validity: A series of five principle component factor analysis with varimax rotations consistently indicated a three factor model for the measure items.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid given that alpha reliabilities are within the excellent range. However, future research should examine the criterion validity of the measure. In addition, the sample size was large enough for generalizability purposes.
entries.source: Mulac, A. (1975). Evaluation of the speech dialect attitudinal scale. Speech Monographs, 42, 184-189.
entries.sourceApa7: Mulac, A. (1975). Evaluation of the speech dialect attitudinal scale. Speech Monographs, 42(3), 184–189. https://doi.org/10.1080/03637757509375893

entries.name: Teacher Evaluations Of Children’s Speech Patterns
entries.purpose: This measure was created to determine how teachers perceive students based on speech patterns.
entries.numberOfItems: Participants were presented with 17 statements that were then measured using a pair of oppositely worded adjectives. The 17 statements created two unique factors: confidence-eagerness (11 items) and ethnicity-nonstandardness (6 items).
entries.format: There are seven steps between the adjective pairs.
entries.originalSample: The speech samples were created using a diverse group (White, Black, and Mexican American) of 46 fifth and sixth grade boys. One hundred and two teachers then rated 3 of the speech samples.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: Discriminant validity was demonstrated because the measure could discriminate between socio-economic levels with regards to both eagerness and nonstandardness.
entries.critique: Although the instrument appears valid, the authors did not provide reliability coefficients for the instrument. Future research should confirm the two factor structure of the measure.
entries.source: Williams, F., Whitehead, J. C., Traupmann, J. (1971). Teachers’ evaluations of children’s speech. The Speech Teacher, 20, 247-254.
entries.sourceApa7: Williams, F., Whitehead, J. C., & Traupmann, J. (1971). Teachers’ evaluations of children’s speech. The Speech Teacher, 20(4), 247–254. https://doi.org/10.1080/03634527109377897

entries.name: Verbal Immediacy Scale
entries.purpose: This measure is designed to assess student’s perception of instructor use of verbal behaviors that create a perceived psychological closeness.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 20 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 0 (never) to 4 (very often).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 387 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Split half reliability was .98.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated that the 20-items consist of one factor.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and contextually valid as operationalized for the assessment of student’s perception of instructor use of verbal behaviors that create a perceived psychological closeness. Future research should examine the criterion validity of the measure.
entries.source: Gorham, J. (1988) The relationship between verbal teacher immediacy behaviors and student learning. Communication Education, 37, 40-53.

entries.name: Children’s Sadness Management Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine how children manage sadness.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 12 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: inhibition (4 items), emotion regulation coping (5 items), and dysregulated expression (3 items).
entries.format: Three point range from 1 (hardly ever) to 3 (often).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 227 children. The mean age of the sample was 10.8, and 53.30% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: inhibition (α = .77), emotion regulation coping (α = .62), and dysregulated expression (α = .60).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation accounted for 51.5% of the variance in the two factor model.
entries.critique: Although the scale appears valid, two factors had unacceptable and undesirable reliability coefficients. However, one factor had a respectable reliability coefficient. Future research should revise the scale before using.
entries.source: Zeman, J., Shipman, K., & Penza-Clyve, S. (2001). Development and initial validation of the Children’s Sadness Management Scale. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 25, 187-205.

entries.name: Clothing Questionnaire
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess individual’s perception of and relation to clothing.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 17 Likert-type items measuring four subscales: clothing consciousness (8 items), exhibitionism (4 items), practicality (3 items), and designer (2 items).
entries.format: The exact anchors used in the study were not provided.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 371 undergraduate students. 53.37% of the sample was male.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated a four structure model.
entries.critique: Although the sample size is large enough for generalizability purposes, the authors did not provided nor discuss reliability coefficients for the scale. Furthermore, the anchors for the scale are unknown. Future research should confirm alpha reliabilities for the four structure model.

entries.name: Communicative Quality
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine the connotative, denotative, and potency aspects of an individual’s conversations.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 33 semantic differential items measuring three subscales: connotative (10 items), denotative (12 items), and potency (11 items).
entries.format: There are seven steps between the adjective pairs.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 60 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation accounted for 55% of the variance in the three factor model.
entries.critique: First, the sample size is a little small, which could lead to problems accurately factor analyzing the scale items due to sampling adequacy problems. Second, although the factorial validity of the scale has been established, the authors did not provide nor discuss the alpha reliability of the scale nor discuss criterion validity.

entries.name: Emotional Contagion Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to gauge an individual’s susceptibility to others' emotions resulting from afferent feedback generated by mimicry.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 15 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (never) to 5 (always).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 883 participants: 543 undergraduate students, 85 physicians, and 255 US Marines. The mean age of the sample was 25.09, and 60.59% of the sample was male.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .90. Test-retest reliability (after one week) was .84.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated a single factor model. Predictive validity was established by correlating the Emotional Contagion Scale with a range of previously validated measures: affective orientation (r = .29), femininity (r = .42), neuroticism (r = -.30), and empathetic tendency (r = .47).
entries.critique: This measure appears reliable and valid. The sample size was large and diverse and is generalizable. The alpha reliabilities for the scale were good and excellent.
entries.source: Doherty, R. W. (1997). The Emotional Contagion Scale: A measure of individual differences. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 21, 131-154.

entries.name: Revised Nonverbal Immediacy Measure
entries.purpose: This is a shortened measure designed to examine an individual’s perceived physical or psychological closeness with another person as a result of nonverbal behaviors.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 10 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 0 (never) to 4 (very often).
entries.originalSample: The original sample was derived from four different universities in different countries. The sample included 139 Australian students, 431 Puerto Rican students, 151 Finnish students, and 365 United States students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the measure was collected for each country: Australia (α = .79), Puerto Rico (α = .69), Finland (α = .89), and United States (α = .85).
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: While the measure’s face value appears to be measuring the author’s intent, the measure should be further explored to determine the measure’s factorial/construct validity, the measure’s criterion validity, and the measure’s reliability. entries.name: Same Sex Touching Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine people’s perceptions of same-sex touching.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 20 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 62 participants. The mean age of the sample was 44.3, and 53.23% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .98.
entries.validity: Concurrent validity was established by correlating the Same Sex Touch Scale with masculinity (r = -.42) and femininity (r = .32). Discriminant validity was established by demonstrating that the Same Sex Touch Scale was negatively related to same sex touch avoidance (r = -.77) but not related to opposite sex touch avoidance (r = -.10).
entries.critique: This measure appears reliable and valid. The measure produced a high alpha reliability estimate.

entries.name: Teacher Perceptions Of Student Nonverbal Behaviors
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to determine how teachers view their students nonverbally.
entries.numberOfItems: Participants were presented with a series of 36 nonverbal behaviors covering six factors: proxemics (7 items), haptics (8 items), oculesics (4 items), kinesics (4 items), vocalics (5 items), and physical appearance (8 items).
entries.format: Participants were asked to indicate the approximate percentage of students in their grade who engaged in various nonverbal behaviors. They were instructed to mark 100% if virtually all students engaged in the behaviors, 75% if most students engaged in the behavior, 50% if about half engaged in the behavior, 25% if some but not half engaged in the behavior, and 0% if virtually none of the students engaged in the behavior.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 901 elementary and secondary educators.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .93.
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: Although this measure produced a high reliability estimate and is generalizable to other populations, the authors did not provide nor discuss factor structure or validity. Future research should examine the validity of this measure and consider other populations.
entries.source: Andersen, S. F., Andersen, P. A., Murphy, M. A., & Wendt-Wasco, N. (1985). Teachers’ reports of students’ nonverbal communication in the classroom: A developmental study in grades K-12. Communication Education, 34, 292-307.

entries.name: Touch Avoidance Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess the degree to which individuals do not like to be touched.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 18 Likert-type items measuring two factors: same sex touch avoidance (10 items) and opposite sex touch avoidance (8 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 210 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for same sex touch avoidance (TAM1) was .82. Alpha reliability for opposite sex touch avoidance (TAM2) was .74. Test-retest reliability for TAM1 was .61, which increased to .75 when corrected for attenuation. Test-retest reliability for TAM2 was .56, which increased to .69 when corrected for attenuation.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated a two factor model. Predictive validity was established by correlating the Touch Avoidance Measure with communication apprehension: TAM1, r = .15; TAM2, r = .18.
entries.critique: Although this measure produced respectable alpha reliabilities and a generalizable sample, test-retest of the scale items produced minimally acceptable to respectable reliabilities.
entries.source: Andersen, P. A., & Leibowitz, K. (1978). The development and nature of the construct touch avoidance. Environmental Psychology and Nonverbal Behavior, 3, 89-106.

entries.name: Imhof-Janusik Listening Concepts Inventory
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine how people understanding the concept of listening.
entries.numberOfItems: Participants are provided with 65 statements that they may perceive to be similar to listening measuring four subscales: organizing information (8 items), relationship building listening (7 items), learning and integrating information (11 items), and critical listening (7 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (not at all similar to listening) to 5 (identical with listening).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 354 undergraduate students: 204 from the United States and 154 from Germany.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: organizing information (α = .87), relationship building listening (α = .90), learning and integrating information (α = .90), and critical listening (α = .87).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation accounted for 47.06% of the variance in the three factor model.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. The measure produced high reliability estimates. This measure is generalizable in the United Sates and Germany.

entries.name: Listening Barriers Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine the degree to which individuals report suffering from specific barriers to listening.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 13 Likert-type items broken into six subscales: laziness (2 items), closed minded (2 items), opinionated (3 items), insincerity (2 items), boredom (3 items), and inattentive (2 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (most of the time) to 5 (never).
entries.originalSample: 279 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: The original 25 item version of scale (pre-factor analysis) had an alpha reliability of .79. However, alpha reliability information was not provided after the factor analysis.
entries.validity: The six factors were shown to account for 50.6% of the scales variance.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. However, the author did not report scale reliability coefficients after performing factor analysis. Future researcher should examine factor analysis to establish alpha reliability.

entries.name: Protégé Listening Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate protégés’ perceptions of listening and outcomes of the mentoring process.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 22 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: outcomes (11 items), emotional (10 items), and directive listening (3 items).
entries.format: A seven point rating scale was utilized, but the exact anchors were not given in the study.
entries.originalSample: The original sample consisted of 200 first-semester freshmen. All of the freshmen had been assigned an upperclassman mentor to help in the transition to college.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: outcomes (α = .93), emotional (α = .93), and directive listening (α = .79).
entries.validity: Each of the factors were shown to be stable through a principle component analysis. The three factors were shown to be moderately related to one another, which is an indication of construct validity. Another test of construct validity was examining known groups. Since women have been shown to be superior listeners when compared to men, sex differences on the three variables indicated that women reported higher scores.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. The measure produced respectable and excellent estimates of reliabilities.
entries.source: Young, R. W., & Cates, C. M. (2004). Emotional and directive listening in peer mentoring. International Journal of Listening, 18, 21-33.
entries.sourceApa7: Young, R. W., & Cates, C. M. (2004). Emotional and directive listening in peer mentoring. International Journal of Listening, 18(1), 21–33. https://doi.org/10.1080/10904018.2004.10499060

entries.name: The Listening Styles Profile (LSP-16)
entries.purpose: The LSP-16 was designed to assess four approaches to receiving information.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 16 Likert-type items measuring four subscales: people (4 items), action (4 items), content (4 items), and time (4 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 0 (never) to 4 (always).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 1,799 undergraduate students. 55.75% of the sample was male.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: people (α = .62), action (α = .64), content (α = .58), and time (α = .65). Test-retest reliability using a sub-sample (n = 464) after a two week period found the following reliabilities: people (r = .68), action (r = .75), content (r = .73), and time (r = .71).
entries.validity: A principle components analysis with an oblique rotation accounted for 50% of the variance in the four factor structure.
entries.critique: Although this measure appears to be valid, the measure produced undesirable alpha reliabilities for three factors and an unacceptable alpha reliability for one factor. Future research should attempt to improve the reliabilities by confirming the four factor structure of this measure.
entries.source: Watson, K. W., Barker, L. L., Weaver, J. B. III. (1995). The Listening Styles Profile (LSP-16): Development and validation of an instrument to assess four listening styles. International Journal of Listening, 9, 1-13.

entries.name: Communication Satisfaction Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to an individual’s level of communication satisfaction.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 19 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Seven point range from 1 (agree) to 7 (disagree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 252 undergraduate students. The mean age of the sample was 22.
entries.reliability: Reliability was tested using 115 undergraduate students. Fifty eight participants were placed in dyads and asked to rate their communication satisfaction with their partner (α = .97). Fifty seven participants were asked to rate their communication satisfaction of a recent interaction (α = .90).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated one strong factor. No items loaded less than .49 on the factor and none had meaningful loadings on secondary factors. To confirm this structure, a principle component analysis with an oblique rotation was conducted. However, the single factor model was deemed most appropriate. Lastly, concurrent validity was established by having the participants respond to a face scale (series of seven sketched faces which range by degree from positive to negative expressions) about either their actual (r = .87) or recalled interaction (r = .64).
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. The measure produced excellent reliability coefficients for the scale.

entries.name: Attitudes And Attributions To Foot-In-Door Requests
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess a participants’ attitudes and attributions toward persuasive foot-in-the-door requests.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 21 Likert-type items measuring ten factors: good cause (2 items), good principle (1 item), source (2 items), emotional benefit (1 item), appearances and obligations (4 items), self (3 items), time-energy threshold (2 items), task (1 item), activism (2 items), and general environment (3 items).
entries.format: The first 16 items were measured using a 0 to 3 response scale with higher scores indicating that the reason affected their decision to agree to the first request. Items 17-21 were measured using a 1 to 5 response scale to measure how the participants perceive themselves in general. The actual anchors used for the two ranges were not provided.
entries.originalSample: The original sample consisted of 337 participants who were approached by an experimenter in their homes.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: good cause α = .74), good principle (no reliability), source (α = .74), emotional benefit (no reliability), appearances and obligations (α = .82), self (α = .83), time-energy threshold (α = .56), task (no reliability), activism (α = .61), and general environment (α = .68).
entries.validity: A confirmatory factor analysis indicated that a 10 factor solution best explained the 21 items.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. Also, the authors utilized a large sample rendering the measure generaliazble to other populations. However, there are two problematic issues with this measure. First, the authors did not provide the actual anchors used for the two ranges. Without the specific anchors of this measure discussed in the article, replicating this measure in the exact way the authors originally utilized the measure is problematic. Second, the authors did not report alpha reliability for one subscale, alpha reliability for one subscale was unacceptable, one was undesirable, and one was minimally acceptable. Future research should attempt to improve the aforementioned reliabilities.

entries.name: Cognitive Communication Competence
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate four mental processes: 1) anticipation of situational variables that have the potential to influence one's communication behaviors, 2) perception of the consequences of one's communication choices, 3) immediate reflection, and 4) continued reflection upon the choices one has mad.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 22 Likert-type items measuring five subscales: reflection cognitions (5 items), presence cognitions (4 items), planning cognitions (5 items), modeling cognitions (4 items), and consequence cognitions (4 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (never true of me) to 5 (always true of me).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 411 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: reflection cognitions (α = .86), presence cognitions (α = .68), planning cognitions (α = .73), modeling cognitions (α = .71), and consequence cognitions (α = .81).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with an oblique rotation accounted for 57% of the variance in the five factor model
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. The alpha reliabilities for two factors are considered good and two are considered respectable. However, the alpha reliability for one factor is considered minimally acceptable. Future research should attempt to improve alpha reliability of the cognitions’ factor.
entries.source: Duran, R. L., & Spitzberg, B. H. (1995). Toward the development and validation of a measure of cognitive communication competence. Communication Quarterly, 43, 259-275.
entries.sourceApa7: Duran, R. L., & Spitzberg, B. H. (1995). Toward the development and validation of a measure of cognitive communication competence. Communication Quarterly, 43(3), 259–275. https://doi.org/10.1080/01463379509369976

entries.name: Communication Competence
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate the following five dimensions that were developed: (1) affiliation/support, (2) social relaxation, (3) empathy, (4) behavioral flexibility, and (5) interaction management skills.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 36 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 239 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .96.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with an oblique indicated a single factor solution.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a reliable and valid operationalization of the measurement of five dimensions. The alpha reliability of the measure is considered excellent. Future research should use this measure to investigate other populations.

entries.name: Communication Competency Self-Report Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess the appropriateness of communication behaviors within a particular setting (the college environment).
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 19 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (always) to 5 (never).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 41 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: Concurrent validity was established by correlating the CCSR with communication apprehension (r = -.62), argumentativeness (r = .36), and instructor perceptions of competence (r = .70).
entries.critique: First, the sample size is a little small, which could lead to problems accurately factor analyzing the scale items due to sampling adequacy problems. Second, this measure appears to be a valid operationalization of appropriateness of communication behaviors within a particular setting (the college environment), however the author did not report nor discussed the measure’s reliability coefficients. As a result, there is no way to ascertain whether the 19 items are truly measuring one or multiple factors. Future research should clearly evaluate the reliability of the measure.

entries.name: Communication Effectiveness
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to gauge an individual’s perception of her or his own effectiveness as a communicator.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 10 Likert-type items.
entries.format: One-hundred and one point range from 0 (never effective) to 100 (always effective).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 148 undergraduate students. 65.54% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .90.
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a valid operationalization of appropriateness of an individual’s perception of her or his own effectiveness as a communicator. The alpha reliability for the measure is considered excellent. However, the authors did not report nor discussed the measure’s validity in the article. As a result, there is no way to ascertain whether the 10 items are truly measuring one or multiple factors. Future research should clearly evaluate the criterion validity of the measure, and use an exploratory factor analysis to ascertain the structure of the 10 items.

entries.name: Conversational Sensitivity Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to analyze the degree to which an individual is attuned to a conversational situation.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 43 Likert-type items measuring twelve subscales: expectation (4 items), predictability (3 items), mood (2 items), topic familiarity (4 items), acquaintance (3 items), tension (5 items), purpose (4 items), formality (2 items), personal (3 items), affinity (5 items), impression-leaving (4 items), and involvement (4 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The original article consisted of 6 different studies including 418 undergraduate students as participants.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: expectation (α = .65), predictability (α = .83), mood (α = .50), topic familiarity (α = .71), acquaintance (α = .71), tension (α = .85), purpose (α = .69), formality (α = .42), personal (α = .76), affinity (α = .78), impression-leaving (α = .72), and involvement (α = .62).
entries.validity: A variety of factor structures were attempted in this study. Ultimately, a ten factor solution was utilized in the final study.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a reliable and valid operationalization of an individual’s degree of attunement to a conversational situation. The alpha reliabilities for the factors ranged from unacceptable to good. Future research should attempt to improve the measure’s reliabilities, and also ascertain the criterion validity of the measure.

entries.name: Guilt Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine the extent that an individual uses and responds to guilt in interpersonal interactions.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 13 Likert-type items measuring three factors: ease (4 items), use (5 items), and susceptibility (4 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 148 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated a three factor model was appropriate.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a valid operationalization of uses and responses of guilt in interpersonal interactions, although reliability coefficients are unknown. Future research should confirm the three factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Interaction Concern Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess a source’s concern with clarity and support during a communicative interaction.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 6 Likert-type items measuring clarity (5 items) and support (5 items).
entries.format: Seven point range from 1 (not at all true of me) to 7 (very true of me).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 86 undergraduate participants.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for clarity was .87. Alpha reliability for support was .85.
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a reliable operationalization of a source’s concern with clarity and support during a communicative interaction, although the validity of the measure is unknown. The lack of both criterion and factorial/context validity is problematic. Future research using this measure should examine measure’s criterion validity and confirm the two factor structure of the measure.

entries.name: Measure Of Interpersonal Communication Competence
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to asses an individual’s perception of her or his communication competence.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 30 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: self-disclosure , empathy, social relaxation, assertiveness, altercentrism, interaction management, expressiveness, supportiveness, immediacy, and environmental control. Each subscale is measured using 3 items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (almost never) to 5 (almost always).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 477 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: self-disclosure (α = .63), empathy (α = .49), social relaxation (α = .63), assertiveness (α = .72), altercentrism (α = .49), interaction management (α = .41), expressiveness (α = .46), supportiveness (α = .43), immediacy (α = .45), and environmental control (α = .60). Alpha reliability for the entire measure was .86.
entries.validity: Concurrent validity was established by correlating the Interpersonal Communication Competence Measure with two previously validated measures: cognitive flexibility (r = .49) and communication flexibility (r = .40)
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. The alpha reliability for the entire measure is considered very good. However, alpha reliabilities for six factors are considered unacceptable. The alphas ranged from α = .41 to α = .49. The alpha reliabilities for three factors are considered undesirable, whereas alpha reliability for one factor is considered minimally acceptable. Future research should clearly evaluate the criterion validity of the measure, and use an exploratory factor analysis to ascertain the structure of the 30 items.
entries.source: Rubin, R. B., & Martin, M. M. (1994). Development of a measure of interpersonal communication competence. Communication Research Reports, 11, 33-44.

entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess an individual’s perception of her or his communication competence. The scale can be used to evaluate communication competence as a whole or in communication contexts (public, meeting, group, and dyadic) or with targets (stranger, acquaintance, and friend).
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 12 Likert-type items.
entries.format: One-hundred and one point range from 0 (completely incompetent) to 100 (completely competent).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 344 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .92.
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: Although this measure appears reliable with an alpha reliability that is considered excellent, the authors did not report nor discussed the measure’s validity. As a result, there is no way to ascertain whether the 12 items are truly measuring one or multiple factors. Future research should clearly evaluate the criterion validity of the measure, and use an exploratory factor analysis to ascertain the structure of the 12 items.

entries.name: Affinity-Seeking Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to operationalize Bell and Daly’s affinity-seeking typology into a shortened scale.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 7 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 0 (never) to 4 (very often).
entries.originalSample: The sample in this study consisted of undergraduate students, but the exact demographics of the sample were not provided.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .84.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis accounted for 89% of the variance in the single factor model.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. The alpha reliability for the measure is considered good. However, the author did not report nor discussed the sample size nor demographics. Future research using this measure needs to examine the measure’s sample information, as well as confirm the single factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Attentiveness Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess the degree to which an individual is able to tell if communication is working.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 30 Likert-type items measuring four subscales: inactivity (6 items), attentiveness signals (12 items), attentiveness sensitivities (5 items), and attentiveness evaluation (7 items).
entries.format: The exact anchors used in the study were not provided.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 1,086 participants.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: A principal axis factor analysis and McQuitty’s elementary linkage analysis was used to interpret the four factor structure. The four factor solution accounted for 35.7% of the variance. The factor structure stayed consistent under both orthogonal and oblique rotations.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a valid operationalization of the degree to which an individual is able to tell if communication is working. Notably, the sample size was large. However, the authors did not report nor discussed the measure’s reliability coefficients in the article. Future research should confirm the factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Baxter Self-Disclosure Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess the degree of willingness to discuss topics of varying intimacy and valence.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 11 Likert-type items measuring three factors: here and now (4 items), updating (3 items), and broad interests/opinions (4 items).
entries.format: The exact anchors used in the study were not provided.
entries.originalSample: The original sample consisted of 102 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: The reliability coefficients were calculated using Nunally’s formula 6-18. The reliability coefficients reported are as follows: here and now (.82), updating (.76), and broad interests/opinions (.75)
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with an oblique rotation accounted for 80.6% of the variance in the three factor model.
entries.critique: Although this measure produced reliability coefficients that ranged from respectable to good, the exact anchor points of the measure are unknown. Without the specific anchors of this measure discussed in the article, replicating this measure in the exact way the author originally utilized the measure is problematic. Future research should confirm the three factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Communicator Style & Image Scale
entries.purpose: This scale was designed to measure an individual’s perception of her or his communicator style (open, dominant, & relaxed) as well as her or his overall communicative image.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 24 Likert-type items broken into four subscales: open communicator style (4 items), dominant communicator style (4 items), relaxed communicator style (4 items), and communicator image (4 items).
entries.format: Seven point range from 1 (definitely did use) to 7 (definitely did not use).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of real estate salespeople representing over 40 different real estate sales offices in three different states in the United States. The total sample consisted of 152 participants.
entries.reliability: The alpha reliabilities are as follows: open communicator style (α = .71), dominant communicator style (α = .75), relaxed communicator style (α = .76), and communicator image (α = .82).
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable. The Alpha reliabilities for the four factors ranged from respectable to good. However, the authors did not report nor discussed the measure’s validity in this article. As a result, there is no way to ascertain whether the 24 items are truly measuring one or multiple factors. Future research should clearly evaluate the criterion validity of the measure, and use an exploratory factor analysis to ascertain the structure of the 24 items.

entries.name: Communicator Style Scale
entries.purpose: This scale was designed to examine the way one verbally and paraverbally interacts to signal how literal meaning should be taken, interpreted, filtered, or understood.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 51 Likert-type items measuring ten subscales: dominant (5 items), dramatic (5 items), contentious (5 items), animated (5 items), impression leaving (5 items), relaxed (5 items), attentive (5 items), open (5 items), friendly (5 items), communicator image (6 items).
entries.format: Seven point range from 1 (very strong disagreement) to 7 (very strong agreement).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 1,086 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: The alpha reliabilities are based on 500 cases. Alpha reliabilities for the factors were as follows: dominant (α = .82), dramatic (α = .68), contentious (α = .65), animated (α = .56), impression leaving (α = .69), relaxed (α = .71), attentive (α = .57), open (α = .69), friendly (α = .72), communicator image (α = .60).
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable. Notably, the sample size was large. The Alpha reliabilities for the four factors ranged from unacceptable to respectable. However, the authors did not report nor discussed the measure’s validity in this article. As a result, there is no way to ascertain whether the 51 items are truly measuring one or multiple factors. Future research should attempt to improve the low factor reliabilities and clearly evaluate the criterion validity of the measure, and use an exploratory factor analysis to ascertain the structure of the 51 items.

entries.name: Decision Making Collaboration Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess an individual’s general willingness to participate collaboratively in decision-making communication interpersonally.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 13 Likert-type items,
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (almost never true) to 5 (almost always true).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 401 undergraduate students. The mean age of the sample was 20.20, and 54.61% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .81.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation accounted for 51.9% of the variance in the single factor model. Predictive validity was established by correlating the Decision Making Collaboration Scale with a range of previously validated measures: argumentativeness (r = .58), verbal aggression (r = -.19), communication competence (r = .52), and willingness to communicate (r = .43). Construct validity was examined by having individuals rate their own collaboration behavior and having a friend rate their collaboration behavior (r = .52).
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. Notably, the sample size was large. The alpha reliability is considered good. Future research should confirm the single factor structure of this measure.

entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. Notably, the sample size was large. The alpha reliability is considered excellent. Future research should confirm the single factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Interaction Involvement
entries.purpose: The purpose of this measure was to determine the extent to which an individual partakes of her or his social environment.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 18 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: perceptiveness (7 items), other-oriented perceptiveness (7 items), and attentiveness (4 items).
entries.format: Seven point range from 1 (not at all like me) to 7 (very much like me).

entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis for 70.11% of the variance in the three factor model.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. Notably, the sample size was large. The alpha reliabilities for the three factors are considered very good. Future research should confirm the three factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Normative Message Processing Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to differentiate between individuals who engage in message processing that is selective, effortful, and deliberate and message processing that is unselective, low effort, and nondeliberate.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 24 Likert-type items measuring two subscales: analytical (15 items) and intuition (9 items).
entries.format: The exact anchors used in the study were not provided.

entries.critique: Although this measure produced reliability coefficients that ranged from respectable to good, the exact anchor points of the measure are unknown. entries.name: Personal-Enacted Identity Gap Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine the degree to which an individual allows another person to see how the individual views her or himself.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 11 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Seven point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 135 undergraduate students. 54.1% of the sample was female, and 89.6% of the sample was Anglo-Saxon/Caucasian.

entries.name: Sarcasm Self-Report Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess the degree to which an individual is likely to use sarcasm.

entries.name: Sensitivity To Feedback Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess an individual’s sensitivity to feedback.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 19 Likert-type items measuring four subscales: anticipation of response (6 items), sensitivity to socially undesirable feedback (4 items), sensitivity to social desirable feedback (5 items), and sensitivity to attention 4 (items).
entries.format: Six point range from 1 (always false) to 6 (always true).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 250 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: anticipation of response (α = .91), sensitivity to socially undesirable feedback (α = .89), sensitivity to social desirable feedback (α = .90), and sensitivity to attention 4 (α = .85).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation accounted for 60% of the variance in the four factor model. entries.name: Argumentativeness Measure
entries.purpose: The scale was designed to determine the degree to which an individual in communication situations advocates positions on controversial issues and attacks verbally the positions which other people take on these issues.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 6 Likert-type items designed to measure the tendency to approach arguments (ARGap - 10 items) and the tendency to avoid arguments (ARGav - 10 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (rarely true) to 5 (almost always true).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 692 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for ARGap was .91. Alpha reliability for ARGav was .86. Furthermore, a one-week test-retest procedure found the following: ARGap (r = .87) and ARGav (r = .86).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation found that ARGap accounted for 55% of the common variance in the varimax solution and ARGav accounted for 45% of the common variance. Construct validity was tested by examining the relationship between 34 friend pairs where one friend filled out the measure on her or himself and the other friend filled the measure out about their friend. The results for this analysis found a positive relationship for both ARGap (r = .54) and ARGav (r = .42). Evidence of both concurrent and predictive validity are also supplied in the article.
entries.critique: Overall, this measure appears to be reliable and valid. Notable, the sample size was large. The alpha reliabilities for the factors ranged from good to excellent. Future research should confirm the validity of this measure.
