entries.name: Child-Parent Communication Apprehension Scale For Use With Young Adults (C-PCA, YA)
entries.purpose: To measure a young adult child’s fear or anxiety while communicating with her or his father and mother.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 12 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 400 undergraduate students. The mean age of the sample was 20.20, and 59.25% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .90.
entries.validity: C-PCA was found to positively relate to levels of interpersonal CA across all four groupings (mother: male & female participants; father: male & female participants). C-PCA was also negatively related to general parent-child communicative contact across all four groups. Both of these results are indications of concurrent validity. As for predictive validity, the C-PCA was shown to accurately predict a youth’s level of relationship satisfaction with her or his parent.
entries.critique: Overall, this measure appears to be reliable and valid. Notable, the sample size was large. The alpha reliability for the measure is considered good. Future research should confirm the validity of this measure.

entries.name: CMC Apprehension
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine an individual’s level of communication apprehension in three different CMC contexts: e-mail, chatting, and instant-messaging.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 15 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: e-mail (5 items), chatting (5 items), and instant-messaging (5 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 145 undergraduate students. The mean age of the sample was 20.91, and 55.9% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the subscales were as follows: e-mail (α = .88), chatting (α = .91), and instant-messaging (α = .91).
entries.validity: Because the three CMC contexts are highly related, three separate factor analyses were conducted on the different subscales. A principle component factor analysis was conducted on the e-mail subscale and accounted for 67.71% of the variance in the single factor model. A principle component factor analysis was conducted on the chatting subscale and accounted for 73.62% of the variance in the single factor model. A principle component factor analysis was conducted on the instant messaging subscale and accounted for 74% of the variance in the single factor model.
entries.critique: Overall, this measure appears to be reliable and valid. The alpha reliabilities for the subscales ranged from good to excellent. Future research using this measure should confirm the validity of this measure.

entries.name: Personal Report Of Intercultural Communication Apprehension (PRICA)
entries.purpose: To measure an individual’s level of communication apprehension with individuals from different cultures.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 14 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The original sample consisted of 396 undergraduate students. The mean age of the sample was 19.3, and 64.65% of the sample was female.

entries.name: Personal Report Of Spouse Communication Apprehension
entries.purpose: To measure an individual’s level of fear or anxiety while communicating with one’s spouse. The scale can also measure general CA with a relationship partner (Beatty & Dobos, 1993).
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 15 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 214 undergraduate students. The participants reported an average history of 3.2 serious dating relationships.
entries.reliability: Split half reliability was .88.
entries.validity: A factor analysis indicated that the 15 items of the Personal Report of Spouse Communication Apprehension did not factor with McCroskey’s (1970) Personal Report of Communication Apprehension, which indicates that the two are clearly different constructs and provides a level of construct validity. Spousal Communication Apprehension levels (low vs. high) were shown to differ in their desire to assume more communication responsibility, belief that the spousal role requires high Face-to-Face interaction, perception that things were going well with one’s spouse, considerations of separation, marital happiness, and desire to marry the same person, which is an indication of predictive validity.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. The split-half reliability for the measure is considered good. Future research using this measure should confirm the validity of the measure.

entries.name: Unwillingness To Communicate Scale
entries.purpose: To measure the degree to which approach or avoid communication (approach-avoidance) and an individual’s perception of the value of her/his communication with others (reward).
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 20 Likert-type items: 10 items on the approach-avoidance factor and 10 items on the reward factor.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 222 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Split-half reliability for the approach-avoidance factor ranged from .86 to .90. Split-half reliability for the reward factor was .79 to .82. Furthermore, the alpha reliability for the approach-avoidance factor was .80 and .68 for the reward factor.
entries.validity: Communication apprehension positively related with the approach-avoidance factor (r = .69), but CA was not correlated with the reward factor (r = .01), which supports partial construct validity. Further research indicated that the approach-avoidance factor was negatively related to group participation, group information-giving, and group information seeking, but the reward factor was not related to these three variables. The reward factor was negatively related with satisfaction with the group, attraction to group members, and perceived group coordination, while the approach-avoidance factor was not related to these three variables.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be reliable and valid. The alpha reliabilities for the measure factors ranged from minimally acceptable to good. Future research should attempt to improve the low reliability and confirm the four factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Willingness To Communicate Scale (WTC)
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to indicate an individual’s predisposition toward approaching or avoiding the initiation of communication. The scale can be used to evaluate an individual’s willingness to communicate as a whole, in communication contexts (public, meeting, group, and dyadic), or with targets (stranger, acquaintance, and friend).
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 20 possible communication situations. However, only 12 of the items are intended to measure the WTC construct. The scores can be used to examine WTC in specific communicative contexts (public, meeting, group, & dyadic) or with specific communicative targets (stranger, acquaintance, or friend). The measure consists of 20 Likert-type items, but only 12 are used to score the measure.
entries.format: Participants are asked to indicate the percentage of times (0-100%) he or she would choose to communicate in each type of situation.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 1,641 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: The overall alpha reliability for the WTC scale was .92. The alpha reliabilities for the communicative contexts were .74 for public, .70 for meeting, .65 for group, and .68 for dyadic. The alpha reliabilities for the communicative targets were .84 for stranger, .79 for acquaintance, and .76 for friend. In international comparisons (U.S., Sweden, Australia, Micronesia, Finland, & Estonia), the alpha reliabilities ranged from .86 to .92 for the overall WTC scale. In a sample of 174 participants, test-retest reliability was .79 or .86 when corrected for attenuation.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated a single factor model. Concurrent validity was established by correlating the Willingness to Communicate Scale with the Verbal Activity Scale (r = .41) and the Personal Report of Communication Apprehension-24 (r = -.50). Predictive validity was established by correlating the Willingness to Communicate Scale with a range of previously validated measures: self-esteem (r = .22), anomie (r = -.14), alienation (r = -.17), introversion (r = -.29), and self-perceived communication competence (r = .59).
entries.critique: Overall, this measure appears to be reliable and valid. The overall alpha reliability for the scale is considered excellent. In addition, the alpha reliabilities for the factors ranged from undesirably to excellent. Notably, the sample size was very large. Future research should attempt to improve the low reliabilities and confirm the factor structure of this measure.
entries.source: McCroskey, J. C. (1992). Reliability and validity of the willingness to communicate scale. Communication Quarterly, 40, 16-25.

entries.critique: Although this measure appears reliable with an alpha reliability estimate that is considered very good, the authors did not report nor discussed the measure’s validity. However, the problem with this specific sample is that, it is not diverse (homogenous) enough. The information provided in the article shows a large homogenous Anglo-Saxon/Caucasian population. Future research using this measure should clearly examine and confirm the validity of this measure and consider other more diverse populations such as those found in multicultural/multinational work organizations.

entries.name: Mediation Expectation Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to measure disputants and mediators’ perceptions of the mediation process.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 47 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: compliance (8 items), control (9 items), competence (10 items), effectiveness (10 items), and satisfaction (10 items).

entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: compliance (disputant, α = .88; mediator, α = .80), control (disputant, α = .93; mediator, α = .89), competence (disputant, α = .92; mediator, α = .80), effectiveness (disputant, α = .92; mediator, α = .90), and satisfaction (disputant, α = .85; mediator, α = .82).

entries.name: Organizational Dissent Scale
entries.purpose: To measure how employees communicate contradictory opinions and disagreement.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 20 Likert items.
entries.format: Five point ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: 191 employees. The mean age of participants was 39 years. 53% of the sample consisted of men. The average length of job tenure was 8.76 years. Five percent of participants were considered top management, 28% as management, 58% as nonmanagement, and 9% as other (clerical, production, sales).
entries.reliability: Cronbach alphas were .88 for articulated dissent, .76 for latent dissent, and .87 for displaced dissent. Test/retest reliability was .86 for articulated dissent, .79 for latent dissent, and .84 for displaced dissent.
entries.validity: Principal components analysis produced a three factor solution accounting for 50.9% of the variance. Construct validity was established for all three dimensions. Articulated dissent was positively related to workplace freedom of speech, employee satisfaction, organizational commitment, strength of supervisory relationship, perceptions of management’s openness to input, and perceptions of organizational influence. Latent dissent was found to be negatively related to workplace freedom of speech, employee satisfaction, organizational commitment, strength of supervisory relationship, perceptions of management’s openness to input, and perceptions of organizational influence. Displaced dissent was only revealed to be negatively associated with perceptions of organizational influence and organizational commitment.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a reliable and valid operationalization of organizational dissent and has been widely used in subsequent studies. However, Kassing (2000) cautions against using the displaced dimension and provides and alternative operationalization..
entries.source: Kassing, J. W. (1998). Development and validation of the organizational dissent scale. Management Communication Quarterly, 12, 183-229

entries.name: Relational Discrepancy Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess people’s perceptions of how a spouse should behave and how one actually behaves.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 44 Likert-type items measuring 7 subscales: intimacy (17 items), dominance (6 items), receptivity (5 items), informality (3 items), noncomposure/arousal (3 items), distance (3 items), and equality/trust (7 items).
entries.format: The measure uses a seven point scale, but the specific anchors were not provided in the article.
entries.originalSample: The first sample consisted of 215 married individuals attending jury duty. The second sample consisted of 206 married couples living in the southwest. Participants rated how spouses should behave and then how their actual spouse behaves.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: intimacy (ideal spouse, α = .90; actual spouse, α = .89), dominance (ideal spouse, α = .76; actual spouse, α = .75), receptivity (ideal spouse, α = .54; actual spouse, α = .54), informality (ideal spouse, α = .42; actual spouse, α = .67), noncomposure/arousal (ideal spouse, α = .34; actual spouse, α = .42), distance (ideal spouse, α = .68; actual spouse, α = .63), and equality/trust (ideal spouse, α = .85; actual spouse, α = .77).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with an oblimin rotation accounted for 56% of the variance in the seven factor model.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a reliable and valid operationalization of family communication standards although the response format anchors were not provided for the semantic differential scale. Additionally, several subscales produced low reliability estimates.

entries.name: Revised Family Communication Patterns Instrument (RFCP)
entries.purpose: The purpose of this measure was to expand upon Chaffee, McLeod and Wackman’s (1966) concepts of socio and concept oriented family communication patterns.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 26 Likert-type items measuring two subscales: conversation-orientation (15 items) and conformity-orientation (11 items).
entries.format: The exact anchors used in this study were not provided.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 308 interviews with at least one child and at least one parent. All of the children were enrolled in the public school system in Madison, Wisconsin. Responses were obtained from 283 mothers and 211 fathers.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for conversation-orientation was .84. Alpha reliability for conformity orientation was .76.
entries.validity: A factor analysis of the revised measure was not provided in this study. However, family communication pattern understanding was shown to differ across educational cohorts (7th grade, 9th grade, and 11th grade), which is an indication of criterion validity.
entries.critique: Future research should utilize a confirmatory factor analysis of the two factor structure. Furthermore, criterion validity should also be further explored.

entries.name: Hypergender Ideology Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess an individual’s adherence to extremely traditional gender-role ideologies.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 57 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Six point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 297 undergraduate students. The mean age of the participants was 18.71, and 50.05% of the sample was male.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for total sample was .96, for males α = .94, and females α = .92.
entries.validity: A confirmatory factor analysis indicated that a single factor structure was a good fit: CFI = .97 and GFI = .99. Criterion validity was established by correlating the Hypergender Ideology Scale with previously validated measures of hypermasculinity (r = .76) and hyperfemininity (r = .54).
entries.critique: Overall, this measure is a fairly good measure of both hypermasculinity and hyperfemininity. The measure has good reliability and a confirmatory factor analysis clearly indicated a single factor. The only problem with this measure consists of some of the items, which could be perceived as a little abrasive. Furthermore, the sample consisted of undergraduate students, so the generalizability of this measure to other populations is not known.
entries.source: Hamburger, M. E., Hogben, M., McGowan, S., & Dawson, L. J. (1996). Assessing hypergender ideologies: Development and initial validation of a gender-neutral measure of adherence to extreme gender-role beliefs. Journal of Research in Personality, 30, 157-178.

entries.name: Perceived Masculinity Questionnaire
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate masculinity as a social and symbolic construct of communication.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 43 Likert-type items measuring eight subscales: physiological energy (5 items), physical characteristics (6 items), gender-related sociocultural roles (13 items), gender preference (3 items), subjective gender-identity (4 items), gender-related age identity (4 items), gender-related racial/national identities (4 items), and lust (4 items).
entries.format: Each item is measured using seven steps between two anchors. The anchors change to represent each item individually.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 561 undergraduate students. The mode age of the sample was 19, and 54.7% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: physiological energy (α = .79), physical characteristics (α = .34), gender-related sociocultural roles (α = .79), gender preference (α = .65), subjective gender-identity (α = .93), gender-related age identity (α = .54), gender-related racial/national identities (α = -.41), and lust (α = .57).
entries.validity: A maximum likelihood factor analysis with a promax rotation indicated a seven factor model. Predictive validity was established by comparing scores on the Perceived Masculinity Questionnaire between females and males, and males had higher scores.
entries.critique: This measure produces some problematic reliability estimates. The physical characteristics, gender preference, gender-related age identity, and lust subscales produced low reliability coefficients. Most notably, the racial/national identities produced a negative Cronbach’s alpha, which the authors presumed to be a mathematical artifact.

entries.name: Productivity Rating Instrument

entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of five semantic differential items. The basic concept underlying each of the items is clearly defined for each set of adjective pairs.
entries.format: There are seven steps between the adjective pairs ranging from -3 to +3.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 80 undergraduate participants randomly selected to participate in one of twenty work groups.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: Face validity was established by asking five group scholars to examine the definitions associated with the terms provided participants.
entries.critique: The sample consisted of a small sample of undergraduate students, so the generalizability of this measure to other populations is not known. While the measure’s face value appears to be measuring the author’s intent, the measure should be further explored to determine the measure’s factorial/construct validity, the measure’s criterion validity, and the measure’s reliability. This measure appears to be useful, but without the necessary information about the psychometric properties of the measure the scale needs to be reexamined completely.

entries.name: Coping Strategies Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to determine how often individuals have utilized a specific coping strategy in the 6 months prior to the study.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 20 Likert-type items measuring five subscales: positive reappraisal (4 items), cognitive monitoring of emotions (4 items), self/other distancing (5 items), social support/planning (5 items), and faith (2 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 0 (does not apply/never) to 4 (very often).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 96 breast cancer patients.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: positive reappraisal (α = .85), cognitive monitoring of emotions (α = .80), self/other distancing (α = .79), social support/planning (α = .73), and faith (α = .76).
entries.validity: A factor analysis indicated that the five factor model accounted for 56% of the variance.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a valid and reliable operationalization of coping strategies. All subscales produced acceptable reliability estimates. Future research should confirm the five factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Dentist Perception Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine an individual’s perception of communication with one’s dentist (comforting messages & information sharing), an individual’s liking of her or his dentist, and an individual’s perception of the dentist’s technical competence.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 41 Likert-type items measuring four subscales: comforting messages (7 items), information sharing (8 items), interpersonal liking (13 items), and technical competence (13 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (never) to 5 (always).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 236 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: comforting messages (α = .85), information sharing (α = .85), interpersonal liking (α = .94), and technical competence (α = .92).
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article. However, all four factors were found to be negatively related to treatment anxiety: comforting messages (r = -.13), information sharing (r = -.40), interpersonal liking (r = -.40), and technical competence (r = -.54).
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a valid and reliable operationalization of attitudes toward a dentist. All subscales produced acceptable reliability estimates. Future research should confirm the four factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Nurses Decision Making Styles Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was design to examine how nurses make decisions during routine and emergency situations.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 16 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: compliance (6 items), avoidance (5 items), and quickness (5 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 0 (never) to 5 (always).
entries.originalSample: The original sample consisted of 179 nurses at various hospitals with a median age of 31.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors during routine situations were as follows: compliance (α = .82), avoidance (α = .56), and quickness (α = .60). Alpha reliability for the factors during emergency situations were as follows: compliance (α = .77), avoidance (α = .67), and quickness (α = .60).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with an oblique rotation accounted for 82% of the variance in the three factor model. The study found that nurses responded to the scale differently in routine vs. emergency situations, which could be an indication of discriminant validity.
entries.critique: First, the reliability estimates are low for the avoidance and quickness dimensions in both routine and emergency situations. The compliance subscale produced an acceptable reliability estimate. Second, future research should confirm the three factor structure of this scale in a sample of nurses.
entries.source: Wheeless, V. E., Wheeless, L. R., & Riffle, S. (1989). The role of situation, physician communicator style, and hospital rules climate on nurses’ decision styles and communication satisfaction. Health Communication, 1, 189-206.
entries.sourceApa7: Wheeless, V. E., Wheeless, L. R., & Riffle, S. (1989). The role of situation, physician communicator style, and hospital rules climate on nurses’ decision styles and communication satisfaction. Health Communication, 1(4), 189–206. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327027hc0104_1

entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 36 Likert-type items measuring six factors: teachers, high school, studying, study hall, classroom, and school rules.
entries.format: Seven point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 147 12th graders.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: First, this measure is appears relevant to students in high school only (e.g., many items reflect study hall). Second, the internal reliability estimate for the items is unknown. Third, the factor structure of the measure is also unknown.
entries.source: Weaver, C. H. (1959). Semantic distance between students and teachers and its effect upon learning. Speech Monographs, 36, 273-281.

entries.name: Communication Climate In The Classroom Scale
entries.purpose: The scale was designed to measure student perceptions of teacher supportiveness.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 17 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

entries.name: Classroom Climates Questionnaire
entries.purpose: This questionnaire was designed to measure a student’s perception of the supportiveness of a specific classroom environment.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 17 Likert-type items measuring two factors: supportive classroom climate (8 items) and defensive classroom climate (9 items).
entries.format: The range used to measure the 17 items was not provided in the article, but the two anchors were describes my teacher and does not describe my teacher.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 73 high school juniors.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with an orthogonal rotation was used to create the two factor structure.
entries.critique: This measure appears to have a two factor structure representing supportive and defensive climates. Additionally, this measure could be applied to the college classroom as well. However, the internal reliability of both scales was not assessed.

entries.name: Classroom Negotiation Scale
entries.purpose: This scale was designed to assess participants’ perceptions of appropriate and inappropriate negotiation in the classroom.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 12 Likert-type items measuring two factors: student needs (8 items) and challenge (4 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 378 participants: 193 American college students, 75 Korean students studying in the US, and 110 Korean students studying in Korea.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliabilities for the total scale (all 12 items) were as follows: .79 for the American sample, .81 for Korean students in the US, and .79 for Korean students in Korea.
entries.validity: Content validity occurred in three ways: (1) initial discussion with both American and Korean students, (2) face-validity analysis by a series of graduate students and a professor in intercultural communication, and (3) a pilot test of eight Korean and eight American students. Furthermore, a principle component factor analysis accounted for 57.3% of the variance in the two factor model.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a reliable and valid operationalization of classroom negotiation. Notably, this measure has been utilized in two cultures and could be used in additional cultures. Future research should confirm the two factor structure.
entries.source: Yook, E. L., & Albert, R. D. (1998). Perceptions of the appropriateness of negotiation in educational settings: A cross-cultural comparison among Koreans and Americans. Communication Education, 47, 18-29.
entries.sourceApa7: Yook, E. L., & Albert, R. D. (1998). Perceptions of the appropriateness of negotiation in educational settings: A cross-cultural comparison among Koreans and Americans. Communication Education, 47(1), 18–29. https://doi.org/10.1080/03634529809379107

entries.name: Connected Classroom Climate Inventory
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine student-to-student connectedness in a university classroom.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 18 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 565 undergraduate students. The mean age of the sample was 19.71, and 55.93% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .94.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation accounted for 51.33% of the variance in the single factor model. Concurrent validity was established by correlating the Connected Classroom Climate Inventory with three four questions: I feel connected to other students in my class (r = .68), I made friends with other students in my class (r = .64), I would like to enroll in another course with other students in my class if time and schedule permitted (r = .59), and I liked this class because of the students in the class (r = .65).
entries.critique: This measure was shown to be a reliable and valid operationalization of classroom connectedness. Future research should confirm the unidimensional factor structure.
entries.source: Dwyer, K. K., Bingham, S. G., Carlson, R. E., Prisbell, M., Cruz, A. M. et al. (2004). Communication and connectedness in the classroom: Development of the Connected Classroom Climate Inventory. Communication Research Reports, 21, 264-272.

entries.name: Course Evaluation Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine student perceptions of the quality of academic courses.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 20 Likert-type items measuring four subscales: academic motivational and informational effects (8 items), instructor’s interpretation and development of course materials (7 items), interaction leadership (3 items), and instructor’s command of literature (2 items).
entries.format: Seven point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 108 course evaluations from graduate students.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: Face validity was established by an expert panel including twelve faculty and twenty-one graduate teaching assistants. A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation confirmed the creation of a four factor model.
entries.critique: Although a four factor structure was discovered, the internal reliability of the scale is unknown. Future research should confirm the four factor model. This measure may be applicable to the undergraduate classroom as well (especially major specific courses).

entries.name: Course Involvement Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess students perceptions of active involvement in a course.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 36 Likert-type items measuring seven subscales: working hard (7 items), outside of class contact (6 items), refraining from negative behavior (5 items), group citizenship (6 items), positivity (4 items), attendance (4 items), and class discussion (4 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 503 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: working hard (α = .72), outside of class contact (α = .64), refraining from negative behavior (α = .79), group citizenship (α = .84), positivity (α = .63), attendance (α = .82), and class discussion (α = .85).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation accounted for 56% of the variance in the seven factor model.
entries.critique: This measure was shown to be a reliable and valid operationalization of involvement even though several reliability coefficients were on the low side. Future research should confirm the seven factor structure of the measure.
entries.source: Bippus, A. M., & Young, S. L. (2000). What behaviors reflect involvement in a course? Students’ perceptions and differences between high and low communication apprehensives. Communication Research Reports, 17, 310-319.

entries.name: Critical Incidents Frequency Report
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine the frequency of student challenge behavior in the classroom.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 20 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 0 (doesn’t apply) to 4 (very often).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 204 faculty from various universities. 30.2% of the faculty were from Liberal Arts, 26.3% from Education, 24.9% from Math and Sciences, and 18.5% from Business.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .90 for the overall scale. Reliability estimate were .70 for procedural challenges, .84 for evaluation challenges, .66 for power challenges, and .87 for practicality challenges.
entries.validity: Content validity was established as faculty indicated that the challenge behavior items were exhaustive.
entries.critique: This measure was shown to be a valid operationalization of challenge behavior. However, the power challenge subscale produced a low reliability estimate. Future research should confirm the four dimensional factor structure of the measure or a unidimensional solution.

entries.name: Graduate Teaching Assistants’ Concern Check List
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate graduate teaching concerns with their communication in the classroom.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 21 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: teaching and relating to students (11 items), learning the area and resources (6 items), managing time to avoid stress (3 items), and knowing policies and procedures (6 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (not at all concerned) to 5 (concerned a great deal).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 233 graduate teaching assistants participating in a one-week orientation. The mean age of the sample was 27.45, and 52.79% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: teaching and relating to students (α = .84), learning the area and resources (α = .76), managing time to avoid stress (α = .70), and knowing policies and procedures (α = .64).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis accounted for 43% of the variance in the four factor model. Varimax and oblique rotations were identical with a minimal relationship between the factors.
entries.critique: This measure was shown to be a reliable and valid operationalization of graduate teaching assistant concerns. Future research should confirm the four factor structure.

entries.name: Relevance Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to ascertain how relevant course content is to students when trying to apply the content to the “real world.”

entries.name: Being White In America
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to assess non-White individuals’ perceptions that Whites are a distinct, dominant, superior, privileged, and unapproachable racial group in the United States.

entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 447 individuals: 71 White Americans, 206 First Generation Koreans, 116 Korean students, and 54 1 ½-2nd generation Koreans.

entries.name: Communication Approach With The Majority
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to operationalize Orbe’s (1998) Co-Cultural Theory aspect related to how marginalized individuals communicate with people in the majority.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 16 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: assertiveness (6 items), aggressiveness (5 items), and non-assertive (5 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 72 students in Africana studies. The mean age of the sample was 21.65, and 67% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: assertiveness (α = .86), aggressiveness (α = .80), and non-assertive (α = .66).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated a three factor model. Predictive validity was established by predicting relationships between the Communication Approach with the Majority Scale with argumentativeness, verbal aggression, communication apprehension, and perspective taking scale. As a whole the results clearly indicated predictive validity.
entries.critique: Overall, this measure is a reliable and valid measure for measuring Orbe’s (1998) Co-Cultural Theory aspect related to how marginalized individuals communicate with people in the majority. However, the sample consisted of a small group of undergraduate students, so the generalizability of this measure to other populations is not known.

entries.name: Mexican American Cultural Identification Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate participants’ biculturalism.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 26 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: Mexican American Identification (4 items), White American Identification (4 items), Spanish communication (9 items), English communication (6 items), and English radio (3 items).
entries.format: Four point range from 1 (not at all) to 4 (a lot).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 249 7th and 8th grade Mexican Americans living near the California-Mexico border. 51% of the sample was female.

entries.validity: A factor analysis found that the five factor model accounted for 61% of the variance.

entries.name: Self-Construal Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate an individual’s individualistic or collectivistic communication style.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 25 Likert-type items measuring two different concepts: independent self-construal (11 items) and interdependent self-construal (14 items).

entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for independent self-construal was .85. Alpha reliability for interdependent self-construal was .84.
entries.validity: Confirmatory factor analysis for the independent self-construal scale using the 11 items indicated an adequate goodness of fit: NFI = .94, CFI = .96, GFI = .96. entries.critique: While the sample consisted of undergraduate students, so the generalizability of this measure to other populations is not known, the overall measure appears to be both a reliable and valid measure for examining individualistic or collectivistic communication styles. entries.name: Beliefs About Deception
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine an individual’s personal beliefs about deception.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 20 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: intentionality (6 items), deception is wrong (6 items), acceptance of deception (4 items), and upbringing (4 items).
entries.format: Seven point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 321 undergraduate students. The modal age of the sample was 19, and 59.7% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: intentionality (α = .89), deception is wrong (α = .81), acceptance of deception (α = .64), and upbringing (α = .78).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis accounted for 40.38% of the variance in the four factor model. Concurrent validity was established by correlating the four factors with the three factors of Machiavellianism (deceit, trust, & cynicism). All of the relationships were significant.
entries.critique: First, the acceptance of deception subscale produced a low reliability coefficient. However, the remaining subscales appear valid and could be generalizable in other populations. Future research should confirm the four factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Communication Responses To Jealousy Scale (CRJ)
entries.purpose: To measure interactive and behavioral responses to jealousy.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 51 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Seven point, the anchors were not discussed.
entries.originalSample: 363 students or potential jurors (141 men, 222 women) in a dating or marriage relationship. The average age of participants was 23.1 years.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the Interactive Response factors were as follows: active distancing interactive responses (α = .83), negative affect expression (α = .82), integrative communication (α = .83), distributive communication (α = .83), avoidance/denial (α = .75), and violent communication/threats (α = .58). Alpha reliability for the General Behavioral Response factors were as follows: for surveillance/restriction (α = .81), compensatory restoration (α = .80), manipulation attempts (α = .73), rival contacts (α = .78), and violent behavior (α = .67).
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: First, the violent communication/threats and violent behavior subscales produced low reliability coefficients (which may be a function of social desirability bias). Overall, this measure appears be a reliable and valid operationalization of behavioral responses to jealousy. Additionally, the anchor points are unknown for this measure. Future research should confirm the multidimensional factor structure of this measure.

entries.purpose: To measure the meaning of friendship in the elderly population. Number of Items: The scale consists of 27 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

entries.name: General Friendship Inventory-revised (GFI)
entries.purpose: To measure the meaning of friendship in both young and elderly populations while correcting the validity problems with the original 27-item General Inventory of Friendship Intimacy Scale (GIFI) created by Patterson, Bettini, & Nussbaum (1993). Number of Items: Using previous exploratory factor analyses conducted on the 27-item GIFI scale, the authors determined which items loaded using both the younger and older samples. Ultimately, the revised scale consists of 13 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: 249 elderly sample of 68 men and 161 women. The mean age of the sample was 73 years. The young sample of 263 consisted of college students and the general population under the age of 65 years. The average age of this group was 31 years with 97 men and 166 women.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability was .90.
entries.validity: A confirmatory factor analysis using an ordinary least squares confirmatory factor analysis was conducted finding a valid single factor construct. Furthermore, predictive validity was established examining the linear relationships the GFI had with both depression and age.
entries.critique: The GFI appears to be both a reliable and valid measure of friendship intimacy for both adolescent and older populations.

entries.name: Interpersonal Communication Motives Scale

entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 504 participants in five age categories: 25.2% were between 12 and 24, 17.4% were 25 to 34 years, 24% were 35 to 49,26.2% were 50 to 65, and 7.2% were over 65. The mean age of the sample was 40.26, and Males accounted for 44.8% of the respondents. The sample consisted of residents living in three states recruited through undergraduate and graduate research assistants.

entries.format: Six point ranging from 1 (completely or almost completely uncertain) to 6 (completely or almost completely certain)
entries.originalSample: 162 undergraduate students. The mean age of the sample was 20.23, and 70.37% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: For the self uncertainty dimension, Cronbach alphas were .90 for desire, .84 for evaluation, and .89 for goals. For the partner uncertainty dimension, Cronbach alphas were .90 for desire, .85 for evaluation, and .96 for goals. For the relationship uncertainty dimension, Cronbach alphas were .73 for behavioral norms, .89 for mutuality, .86 for definitions, and .88 for future. Composite measures produced alphas of .95 for self uncertainty, .96 for partner uncertainty, and .94 for relationship uncertainty.
entries.validity: Validity was not specifically discussed in this article.
entries.critique: This measure appears to be a reliable and valid operationalization of relational uncertainty. Future research should confirm the multi factor structure of this measure

entries.name: Uses Of Humor Index (UHI)
entries.purpose: To measure three functions of humor in conversation.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 11 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (almost never) to 5 (almost always)
entries.originalSample: 191 students (105 men, 86 women) enrolled in introductory communication courses. Ages ranged from 18 to 31 years with a mean age of 20.
entries.reliability: Cronbach alphas were .72 for the total scale, .61 for positive affect, .71 for expressiveness, and .70 for negative affect.
entries.validity: A principal components analysis was conducted yielding three factors accounting for 54.9% of the variance: positive affect, expressiveness, and negative affect. Convergent validity was established as the UHI correlated positively with another measure of humor. Criterion validity was established as self-report scores on the UHI were correlated positively with peer evaluation scores. Construct validity was established as scores on the UHI were correlated positively with observer coded ratings of interpersonal competence.
entries.critique: The positive affect subscale produced a low reliability estimate. Considering the three factors represent 11 items, future research may involve adding several items to increase the reliability of that subscale. However, multiple types of validity tests established this measure as a valid operationalization of uses of humor.
entries.source: Graham, E. E., Papa, M. J., & Brooks, G. P. (1992). Functions of humor in conversation: Conceptualization and measurement. Western Journal of Communication, 56, 161-183.

entries.name: Advertisement Evaluation Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate an individual’s attitude about a target advertisement.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 10 semantic differential items measuring three subscales: attitude toward ad (5 items), believability (3 items), and readability (2 items).
entries.format: There are seven steps between the adjective pairs.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 249 7th and 8th grade Mexican Americans living near the California-Mexico border. 51% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: attitude toward ad (α = .91), believability (α = .70), and readability (α = .86).
entries.validity: A factor analysis found that the three factor model accounted for 76% of the variance.
entries.critique: The original measure was specifically designed to evaluate adolescents’ perceptions of a an anti-tobacco messages. This measure could be utilized to evaluate other forms of advertising messages, however the exact utility of this measure in other contexts is not known. Furthermore, the original sample was a highly specialized sample, so how this measure would function with other populations is not known. Lastly, the only type of validity discussed in the article was the factor analysis, which really did not receive too much attention in the article. Ultimately, this measure would need to be completely evaluated to ascertain the actual validity of the measure.

entries.name: Audience-Persona Interaction Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate individual’s perceptions of favorite television characters.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 22 Likert-type items measuring four subscales: identify with character (6 items), interest in favorite character (6 items), group identification/interaction (6 items), and favorite character problem solving abilities (4 items).
entries.format: The exact anchors used in the study were not provided.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 417 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: identify with character (α = .87), interest in favorite character (α = .79), group identification/interaction (α = .83), and favorite character problem solving abilities (α = .85).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with a varimax rotation accounted for 49.4% of the variance in the four factor model.
entries.critique: First, the sample consisted of undergraduate students, so the generalizability of this measure to other populations is not known. Second, without the specific anchors of this measure discussed in the article, replicating this measure in the exact way the authors originally utilized the measure is problematic. We suspect that the authors probably used a standard 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) anchoring scheme, but other anchoring schemes could also be utilized. Overall, this measure could be utilized in a variety of different studies that involve the examination of viewers’ perceived interaction with television personas.

entries.name: Consumption Of Media & Advertising
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to evaluate an individual’s consumption of media and attention to advertising.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 5 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 411 participants coming out of two grocery stores in Austin, Texas.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated a single factor model.
entries.critique: Overall, the five items used in this measure appear to be a good measure of simple media consumption. However, the measure does have a couple of major problems. First, there is little information given in the article about the actual participant makeup used in the study. Beyond noting that the two grocery stores existed in different city locations (one urban & one suburban), no information is given about the actual sample. Second, the lack of a reliability estimate for the five items is also concerning. Lastly, the information on the principle component factor analysis is also limited. The authors note that the factor had one eigenvalue above one (eigenvalue = 2.268284), but no information on how much variance that single factor accounts for is given in the article. Furthermore, the authors note that all of the items loaded on the single factor above .54, but the exact loadings are not given.

entries.name: Cultivation Effect Measure
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to determine to what extent an individual’s television viewing can account for a biased perception of the world.
entries.numberOfItems: Participants are asked a series of 13 questions measuring three factors: crime (5 items), marital discord (4 items), and occupational prevalence (4 items).
entries.format: For each item, participants are asked to report the percentage a phenomenon occurs in the real world - from 0 to 100% of people.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 45 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: crime (α = .69), marital discord (α = .71), and occupational prevalence (α = .93).
entries.validity: Predictive validity was established by demonstrating that the amount of soap opera watching an individual does was positively related to all three factors: crime (r = .31), marital discord (r = .56), and occupational prevalence (r = .28)
entries.critique: The items in this measure were derived at through a content analysis of television shows, however the items were not subjected to a confirmatory factor analysis, so there is no way to determine if the 13 items are measuring the three factors. Furthermore, the sample relied on 45 undergraduate students, so the measure may not be generalizable to other participant populations. While the measure has some statistical concerns, the predictive validity is definitely promising.

entries.name: Gratifications Sought
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine an individual’s perception of the gratifications of specific communicative channels in the workplace.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 12 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: production communication (4 items), maintenance communication (4 items), and innovation/adaptation communication (4 items).
entries.format: Four point range from 1 (not at all) to 4 (a lot).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 241 key informants in for-profit organizations. The participants evaluated both their gratifications sought and their gratifications obtained through face-to-face communication, memos, and new technology.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: A confirmatory factor analysis indicated that the three factor model was a good fit across all of the communication contexts.
entries.critique: Overall, this measure appears to be fairly structurally sound. While the lack of reliability information for the three factors is problematic, the confirmatory factor analysis is at least an indication that the items on the three factors group together. However, the fit indexes for two of the contexts (gratifications sought and gratifications obtained through face-to-face) were in the upper .80s but below the standard cutoff of .90. The other two contexts (gratifications obtained through memos and new technology) were both above .90. While the goodness of fit indicators are a little mixed, the structure does appear to be fairly consistent.

entries.name: Media Use Questionnaire
entries.purpose: The purpose of this measure was to examine how people utilize news paper and television content.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 15 Likert-type items. Three categories (5 items each) were examined and each category had two factors. The first category was newspaper content and consisted of two sub-scales: newspaper news (3 items) and newspaper soft news (2 items). The second category was television content and consisted of two sub-scales: television news (3 items) and television entertainment (2 items). The final category was gratifications sought and consisted of two sub-scales: surveillance (2 items) and communicative utility (3 items).
entries.format: Four point range from 1 (never) to 5 (frequently).
entries.originalSample: The sample was achieved using a stratified cluster sampling technique and yielded 364 participants. All participants participated in a telephone survey.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not reported.
entries.validity: A series of factor analyses indicated that the two factor solutions for each subscale could account for substantial variance: 66% of the variance was accounted for by the news paper items, 59% of the variance was accounted for by the television items, and 65% of the variance was accounted for by the gratification items.
entries.critique: Overall, this measure appears to consist of three factors, however the lack of a confirmatory factor analysis does make this measure a little questionable. The authors didn’t factor the measure as a single measure, but opted to factor what they perceived to be individual factors separately. Furthermore, the lack of reported internal reliability for the measure and subscales leads to a possible vulnerability in this measure. Lastly, the lack of clear validation beyond factorial validity could also make this measure problematic in future studies.

entries.purpose: To assess children’s moral reasoning about interpersonal violence.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 12 brief stories about violence. Four of the stories dealt with stealing, four dealt with physical violence, and four dealt with killing someone. Within each category of story, two stories dealt with justifiable violence and two stories dealt with unjustifiable violence. For measurement purposes, each story was rated by the participant and these ratings were treated as individual interval scale items.
entries.format: Seven point ranging from 1 (very, very wrong) to 7 (very, very right)
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 156 children. 71 children were 5 to 8 years old, 50 were 9 to 10 years old, and 35 were between 11 and 12 years old. 55% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Internal reliability estimates were .80 for justified violence and .70 for unjustified violence. Kappa values ranged from .92 to 1.00.
entries.validity: A principal components analysis yielded two factors explaining 65.7% of the variance. Children who watched fantasy violence viewed justified violence as less wrong while children who watched realistic violence viewed it as more wrong.
entries.critique: When using this measure with children, the existence of the 12 stories could be problematic for younger children due to possible attention span problems. Overall, this measure was shown to be both reliability and valid in this study.

entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: accuracy/truth (α = .88), representativeness/ expertise (α = .73), and perspective/bias (α = .75).
entries.validity: A principle component analysis with a varimax rotation found that the three factor model accounted for 54.2% of the variance.

entries.name: Religious Television Viewing Motives
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to gauge an individual’s motivation for watching religious television.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 22 Likert-type items.
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 590 viewers of religious television. The mean age of the sample was 56.95, 67.1% of the sample was female, and 54.3% were African American.
entries.reliability: Reliability coefficients were not presented in this article.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with an oblique rotation indicated that a six factor model accounted for 52.8% of the variance in the 22 items. To reduce error as a result of multicollinearity, structure coefficients were computed by summing the product of canonical loadings and standardized scores of the variables for each set. Ultimately, the canonical correlation extracted three significant roots, which were labeled: reactionary, ritualized, and instrumental. However, the specific items associated with each root was not clearly discussed.
entries.critique: Overall, the statistical methods the author used to arrive at the three significant roots is methodologically sound. However, the lack of reported reliability coefficients is problematic. Furthermore, the author should have also indicated which of the 22 items ultimately loaded on the three roots within the study. Future research in this study, should utilize a confirmatory factor analysis to ascertain the consistency of both the six factor structure and the three root structure.

entries.name: Cancer Information Service Innovation Survey
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to test innovation within the Cancer Information Service.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 20 Likert-type items measuring six subscales: innovativeness (4 items), acceptance (4 items), communication quality (4 items), slack resources (3 items), formalization (3 items), and decentralization (2 items).
entries.format: An 11 point range was used to measure the measure items. However, the exact anchors used in the study were not provided.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 79 members of the geographically dispersed Cancer Information Service.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: innovativeness (α = .86), acceptance (α = .86), communication quality (α = .89), slack resources (α = .69), formalization (α = .62), and decentralization (α = .80).
entries.validity: A confirmatory factor analysis indicated that the six factor model was a good fit (χ2 = 62.12, df 165).
entries.critique: While this measure was specifically designed to examine participants’ perceptions of innovation at the Cancer Information Services, the measure could be used to examine stakeholders perceptions of innovation in other organizations. The measure does have to notable problems. First, the authors did not report the anchors utilized in the measuring of the scale items. Without the specific anchors of this measure discussed in the article, replicating this measure in the exact way the authors originally utilized the measure is problematic. We suspect that the authors probably used a standard 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) anchoring scheme, but other anchoring schemes could also be utilized. Second, the alpha reliability for formulation is undesirable and the alpha reliability for slack resources is minimally acceptable. Future studies should attempt to improve the reliabilities. The low reliabilities could also be attributed to the small sample size. Furthermore, there is not a clear indication that the sample size was adequate for performing a confirmatory factor analysis.

entries.name: Organizational Assimilation Index
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine the degree to which employees feel they have been assimilated into their organizations.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 20 Likert-type items measuring six subscales: supervisor familiarity (3 items), acculturation (3 items), recognition (4 items), involvement (4 items), job competency (4 items), and role negotiation (2 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 342 employees. The mean age of the sample was 32.69, and 64% of the sample was female.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: supervisor familiarity (α = .73), acculturation (α = .73), recognition (α = .86), involvement (α = .72), job competency (α = .62), and role negotiation (α = .64).
entries.validity: A confirmatory factor analysis indicated that the six factor model was a good fit: IFI = .92, CFI = .92, & GFI = .90. Criterion validity was established by correlating the Organizational Assimilation Index with previously validated measures of job satisfaction, propensity to leave, and organizational identification. All six factors of the Organizational Assimilation Index were positively related to job satisfaction and organizationally identification and negatively related to propensity to leave.
entries.critique: Overall, this measure has both factorial and criterion validity. However, the reliability of the measure is mixed, containing factors that are good and minimally acceptable. Future research may want to improve the reliability of some of the factors by increasing the number of items used to measure low performing factors.

entries.name: Organizational Charlatan Scale
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine employee behaviors associated with perceived performance levels at the expense of those associated with actual performance levels.

entries.name: Organizational Communication Support Behaviors
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine mentoring in higher education.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 16 Likert-type items measuring three factors: mentor/protégé (10 items), social/colleague (4 items), and task/colleague (3 items).
entries.format: The anchors used in this study were not provided.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 224 university professors at one public and one private university. 41% of the sample were professors, 45% were associate professors, and 14% were assistant professors.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors during routine situations were as follows: mentor/protégé (α = .87), social/colleague (α = .88), and task/colleague (α = .75).
entries.validity: A principle components factor analysis was conducted with an oblique rotation. The three factor model accounted for 54% of the variance.
entries.critique: First, the article did not indicate the specific anchors used to measure the individual items. Without the specific anchors of this measure discussed in the article, replicating this measure in the exact way the authors originally utilized the measure is problematic. We suspect that the authors probably used a standard 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) anchoring scheme, but other anchoring schemes could also be utilized. Furthermore, the measure is both reliable and indicates factorial/context validity. However, the article did not discuss the measure’s criterion validity, so future research needs to investigate the measure’s criterion validity. Furthermore, future research should also utilize a confirmatory factor analysis to reexamine the three factor structure of the proposed model.

entries.name: Organizational Culture Scale
entries.purpose: To assess an individual’s perception of her or his organizations overarching culture.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 30 Likert-type items measuring five subscales: atmosphere (6 items), involvement (6 items), communication (5 items), supervision (8 items), and meetings (5 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (to a very little extent) to 5 (to a very great extent).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 138 participants in a manufacturing business and 195 participants in a governmental agency.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliabilities for the factors were as follows: atmosphere (α = .77), involvement (α = .88), communication (α = .72), supervision (α = .91), and meetings (α = .63).
entries.validity: A principal component factor analysis with a varimax rotation indicated that a six factor structure was the most appropriate fit. However, the last factor had only one item that significantly loaded on the factor and was dropped from subsequent analysis
entries.critique: First, the article did not report the amount of variance accounted for by the six factor structure. Secondly, the article did not re-run the factor analysis after the one item was dropped from the analysis. Next, the article does not address criterion validity. Lastly, the reliability of the meetings factor is undesirable. Future research should clearly evaluate the reliability of the measure, the criterion validity of the measure, and use a confirmatory factor analysis to further investigate the consistency of a five factor structure of this measure.

entries.name: Organizational Dissent Scale (ODS)
entries.purpose: To measure how employees communicate contradictory opinions and disagreement.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 20 Likert items.
entries.format: Five point ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: 191 employees. The mean age of participants was 39 years. 53% of the sample consisted of men. The average length of job tenure was 8.76 years. Five percent of participants were considered top management, 28% as management, 58% as nonmanagement, and 9% as other (clerical, production, sales).
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: articulated dissent (α = .88), latent dissent (α = .76), and displaced dissent (α = .87). Test/retest reliability was .86 for articulated dissent, .79 for latent dissent, and .84 for displaced dissent.
entries.validity: Principal components analysis produced a three factor solution accounting for 50.9% of the variance. Criterion validity was established for all three dimensions. Articulated dissent was positively related to workplace freedom of speech, employee satisfaction, organizational commitment, strength of supervisory relationship, perceptions of management’s openness to input, and perceptions of organizational influence. Latent dissent was found to be negatively related to workplace freedom of speech, employee satisfaction, organizational commitment, strength of supervisory relationship, perceptions of management’s openness to input, and perceptions of organizational influence. Displaced dissent was only revealed to be negatively associated with perceptions of organizational influence and organizational commitment.
entries.critique: Overall, this measure was shown to be both reliable and valid (factorial/context and criterion). This measure could be useful in other contexts where dissent between people on different rungs of a hierarchy occurs: teacher-student relationships, parent-child relationships, etc…
entries.source: Kassing, J. W. (1998). Development and validation of the organizational dissent scale. Management Communication Quarterly, 12, 183-229

entries.name: Organizational Orientations
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine an individual’s perception of her or his life with respect to work.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 46 Likert-type items measuring three subscales: upward mobile (18 items), ambivalent (16 items), and indifferent (12 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 265 undergraduate students.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the factors were as follows: upward mobile (α = .84), ambivalent (α = .89), and indifferent (α = .79).
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis indicated a three factor model. Criterion validity was established by correlating the Organizational Orientations Scale with a range of previously validated measures: job satisfaction (ambivalent, r = -.49; indifferent, r = -.22; & upward mobile, r = .24), extraversion (ambivalent, r = -.14; indifferent, r = -.03; & upward mobile, r = .16), neuroticism (ambivalent, r = .21; indifferent, r = .19; & upward mobile, r = -.16), and psychoticism (ambivalent, r = .42; indifferent, r = .32; & upward mobile, r = -.37).
entries.critique: Overall, this measure was shown to be both a reliable and valid measure of ambivalent, indifferent, and upwardly mobile organizational orientations. Future research should reanalyze the measure’s three factor structure using a confirmatory factor analysis.

entries.name: Perceived Usefulness of Information Among New Employees
entries.purpose: To understand new organizational members perceptions of the usefulness of the information being provided them within an organization.
entries.numberOfItems: The measure consists of 40 Likert-type items measuring seven subscales: technical (5 items), referent (6 items), social (7 items), appraisal (5 items), normative (7 items), organizational (6 items), and political (4 items).

entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 117 graduates of a business school 6 months after graduation. The sample consisted of 50% females, and the mean age was 24.9. Additionally, 298 MBA students were also utilized for the purposes of factor analyzing the 40 scale items.
entries.reliability: While alpha reliabilities were not individually reported for the separate factors, the authors did note that reliability coefficients were between .74 and .91.

entries.purpose: This measure was designed to examine an individual’s perception of her or his interaction with a service provider.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 24 Likert-type items measuring two subscales: personal connection (12 items) and courteous expression (12 items).
entries.format: Five point range from 1 (never) to 5 (all of the time).
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 256 undergraduate students. 73% of the sample was female, and 67.6% of the sample was Anglo-Saxon/Caucasian.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for personal connection was .91. Alpha reliability for courteous expression was .94.
entries.validity: A principle axis factor analysis with an oblique rotation accounted for 78% of the variance in the two factor model. Concurrent validity was established by correlating the Service Provider Sociality Scale with a range of previously validated measures: customer satisfaction (personal connection, r = .51; courteous expression, r = .86) and customer loyalty (personal connection, r = .47; courteous expression, r = .82).
entries.critique: Overall, this measure was shown to be both a reliable and valid measure of service providers use of personal connection and courteous expression with customers. Future research should use a confirmatory factory analysis to ascertain the consistency of the two factor structure.

entries.name: Telephone Apprehension Measure (TAM)
entries.purpose: To measure communication anxiety associated with using a telephone.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 18 Likert items.
entries.format: Five point ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree)
entries.originalSample: 371 undergraduate students
entries.reliability: Cronbach alpha was .94
entries.validity: Content validity was established using focus groups and expert judges rating items. Concurrent validity was established by discovering a negative correlation between self-reports of average daily phone calls and TAM scores. Construct validity was established by positively correlating TAM scores with a measure of communication apprehension and receiver apprehension.
entries.critique: No information in the article was provided to demonstrate factorial/context validity. While the criterion validity was established and the measure was shown to have excellent reliability, future research should include an exploratory factor analysis to determine if the measure is truly a single factor construct.

entries.name: Training Impact Questionnaire
entries.purpose: This measure was designed to measure trainees’ perceptions of training and development sessions.
entries.numberOfItems: The scale consists of 20 Likert-type items measuring two subscales: relationship of training to job (10 items) and skilled performance (10 items).
entries.format: The exact anchors used in the study were not provided.
entries.originalSample: The sample consisted of 267 individuals who took part in an information technology training session.
entries.reliability: Alpha reliability for the 20-item measure was .88.
entries.validity: A principle component factor analysis with an oblique rotation accounted for 35% of the variance in the two factor model. Predictive validity was determined by correlating scores on the Training IQ with source credibility (r = .73).
entries.critique: First, the amount of variance accounted for by the two factor model is very low for a 20 item measure. Second, only an alpha reliability for the total measure using all 20 items was reported in the article despite the fact that the article clearly discusses two theoretical factors. Third, the article did not indicate the specific anchors used to measure the individual items. Without the specific anchors of this measure discussed in the article, replicating this measure in the exact way the authors originally utilized the measure is problematic. We suspect that the authors probably used a standard 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) anchoring scheme, but other anchoring schemes could also be utilized. Future research should more clearly examine the factor structure of the model using a confirmatory factor analysis, which should be followed by a discussion of the factor(s) alpha reliabilities.
